title: Packers Winners and Losers: Problems Start at the Top Against Rams
full_text:
The Green Bay Packers were in a must-win game on their Thanksgiving Eve matchup with the Los Angeles Rams. Both teams entered the game with 6-4 records. A win would have given the Packers a one-game lead in the standings as well as the all-important tiebreaker in the race for the final playoff spot.
The teams were deadlocked at 13 apiece at halftime in Micah Parsons’ return to the field.
The second half saw Blake Corum and the Rams’ run game grind the Packers’ defense into a bloody pulp. The offense couldn’t muster anything without Christian Watson on the field, as they mustered just two first downs in the second half before Jordan Love threw a back-breaking interception. As a result, the Packers are 6-5 and face an uphill climb to make the postseason.
That reflects poorly on the top two men in the organization, and they lead off our list of winners and losers.
If Jordan Love was going to be in the MVP conversation, that ended with consecutive bad games. Love struggled against Minnesota, but so did the entire offense.
Against the Rams, Love had a chance at redemption. He looked rattled by the pressure from the Rams’ defense even though pass protection held up for the most part.
On the pass that got Christian Watson injured, Kam Kinchens was ejected. Love threw a pass that led Watson into that hit.
Later in the game, it may have been a miscommunication, but Love threw a terrible interception after Ty’Ron Hopper snatched back momentum for the Packers.
If that one wasn’t his fault, his second interception of the game was. He nearly threw another one earlier in the game to Trent McDuffie that he was fortunate hit the turf before McDuffie could corral it.
Love and his team are 6-5. They have not been above the seventh seed in his three seasons as a starting quarterback. Now, the Packers have just a 14 percent chance of making the playoffs, according to the playoff odds shared on the Netflix broadcast.
The Packers are regressing. Wins and losses are not a quarterback stat, but it is what quarterbacks are ultimately judged by. The Packers have not been good enough, and that has included Love in some of the biggest games.
The storylines surrounding Matt LaFleur have been discussed a bunch since the 2025 season ended in disaster in Chicago.
LaFleur was ultimately given a vote of confidence from team president and CEO Ed Policy with a contract extension despite finishing last season with a five-game losing streak. However, his teams look pretty similar to the last three that came before them.
They are capable of great moments, mind-numbing inconsistency and shrinking in the biggest games of the year.
The last two games are a perfect example. LaFleur’s offense was only able to muster 10 points against Brian Flores and the Vikings. Without Christian Watson, LaFleur’s offense turtled against the Rams’ defense.
The Packers are 6-5 this season. All five of their losses are to NFC opponents that are in the playoff hunt. What gives anyone any confidence that the Packers would be able to bounce back and win any big games against a playoff team that is at reasonably full strength?
That’s where the Packers are at this point. They signed up for more of what they saw a season ago. Would the Packers eat LaFleur’s contract extension at the end of a non-playoff season the way 2026 is trending to be?
If losing to the franchise’s biggest rival in the postseason in embarrassing fashion was not enough, that feels unlikely.
This was dangerously close to that four-letter S-word that no football player wants to be referred to. The two most basic principles in the NFL are running the football and stopping the run. The Packers ran for 55 yards. That was not much of a surprise. The Packers cannot run on anybody.
Stopping the run? The Packers had been solid in that department this year, but their run defense betrayed them against Los Angeles. The Rams, who were missing their top three offensive weapons and two starting linemen, piled up 241 yards on the ground, with Blake Corum popping them for 184 yards on 32 carries.
The first drive of the second half was a tone-setter for the rest of the game. The Rams took the ball tied at 13 apiece. They held the ball for 8:02 of game clock. The Packers did not get the ball back until there was 6:58 remaining. The time of possession numbers as a result were 40:40 to 19:20 in favor of the Rams.
Wednesday's game was the equivalent of the Packers knowing what is coming but still being unable to stop it. There's nothing more demoralizing for a defense than to be physically dominated in the way the Packers were. To add insult to injury, the Packers were facing a team without two starting offensive linemen, and they had two more hobbled during the game as well.
The final score does not tell the whole story for how badly the Rams bullied the Packers, who were far too soft in a huge game.
Tucker Kraft’s disappointing season continues. The first half saw him fumble and have a costly drop.
Kraft was the last of four major contract extensions given out by the Packers this season, and he’s in contention with defensive tackle Devonte Wyatt as the least impactful of the bunch.
Wyatt’s lack of impact can be masked thanks to some of the other players on the roster. Kraft’s can’t. He’s the only tight end on the roster capable of making an impact.
He’s not just not making plays in the passing game, he’s making catastrophic mistakes. Maybe the fumble was a great play by linebacker Nate Landman, but it’s a play that cannot happen from an offensive captain. The drop is a play that cannot happen when the Packers are swimming upstream against a vicious Rams’ front.
When Christian Watson left the lineup, the Packers needed Kraft to emerge
The Rams were missing their top two receivers on Wednesday, but with the way that Matthew Stafford abused Keisean Nixon, you may never have known it.
On the Rams’ touchdown drive in the third quarter, Nixon was beaten for two third-down conversions, including a third-and-11.
The man who beat him was not Davante Adams or Puka Nacua, it was Konata Mumpfield. Nothing against Mumpfield as a player, but that’s not a player who can beat you in an obvious passing situation.
Nixon has been good this season, but Wednesday’s homecoming was not his best performance.
With Christian Watson on the sideline for the second half due to a concussion, the Packers’ passing game was down to just two members of their less-is-more passing game.
Jayden Reed is out for the season after a neck injury. Watson leaving the game late in the first half meant that the passing game was left to Matthew Golden and Tucker Kraft.
Kraft is in the midst of arguably his worst season as a pro. Golden appeared to have some sort of miscommunication on an interception by Jordan Love in the third quarter.
Savion Williams, J. Michael Sturdivant and Bo Melton didn’t make enough plays, and the Packers were unable to find any rhythm on offense in the second half.
It’s been a long road, but it did not take long for Micah Parsons to reintroduce himself to the world. On the field for nine passing plays in the first half, he had a sack in which he showed the all-world speed and explosiveness that made him one of the best players in the sport.
Considering the state of some of the other Packers on the roster and their questionable returns from serious injuries like the one Parsons had, his return was a sight for sore eyes.
The Packers are thrilled to have their best player back, and he showed why on Wednesday night.
With the Packers trailing 20-13 with 4:34 left in the third quarter, the Rams’ offensive line was starting to lean on Green Bay’s defense.
Any points from the Rams would have been a devastating punch handed outby their offense. Matthew Stafford dialed up a play-action pass, but the throw did not find its intended target.
Ty’Ron Hopper, who has played well in the absence of Zaire Franklin, made another big play, picking off Matthew Stafford and giving the Packers a second…

title: Rams Beat Packers, Run Them Almost Out of Playoff Race
full_text:
Micah Parsons is in. The Green Bay Packers are out.
Or almost out in terms of the playoff race.
The Los Angeles Rams overpowered the Packers 26-13 on Wednesday night at SoFi Stadium. While Parsons made his long-awaited season debut and was impactful at times, the Packers were run over by Blake Corum during the second half and doomed by an impotent, sloppy offense.
It might wind up being a killer loss for Green Bay. The Packers, Rams and Seahawks entered Week 12 with 6-4 records. The Rams are 7-4 with a one-game lead in the standings but in reality a two-game lead with the head-to-head tiebreaker. The Seahawks will visit the NFC-leading 49ers on Sunday.
The Packers entered the game with a 40 percent chance of reaching, according to The Athletic’s playoff simulator. With a win, that would have increased to 61 percent. Instead, with a loss, it’s down to 25 percent.
A horrendous interception by Jordan Love with 3:39 to go ended the game – and maybe Green Bay’s postseason dreams. From there, Corum continued to turn the Packers into turkeys. His 9-yard run at the 2-minute warning gave the Rams 242 rushing yards, with 184 by Corum. The Packers had only 240 yards of total offense.
After a strong first half, Love was just 17-of-29 for 198 yards with two interceptions. Matthew Golden couldn’t carry the passing attack, catching 1-of-5 targets. Green Bay was 2-of-8 on third down.
With the score tied at 13 at halftime, the Rams embarked on a 15-play, 68-yard scoring drive to open the second half. Blake Corum carried the ball nine times on the drive, including a leg-churning, 1-yard touchdown run. The Rams converted four times on third down, including Matthew Stafford’s 20-yard completion on third-and-8 to Konata Mumpfield against Keisean Nixon during one of the rare occasions Micah Parsons was kept at bay on a true dropback pass.
The Packers needed an answer but, with Christian Watson out with a concussion, they went three-and-out. They were fortunate to have punted as Jordan Love’s third-down pass was thrown right to Quentin Lake.
The Packers had their chance to turn the game around when linebacker Ty’Ron Hopper got in the passing lane between Matthew Stafford and Tyler Higbee for an interception and return to the Rams’ 43. However, one play later, Love went deep to Matthew Golden but they weren’t on the same page, leading to safety Jaylen McCollough catching the easiest of his five career interceptions.
It was a killer mistake. The third quarter ended with the Rams on the move. During those 15 minutes, they ran 23 plays for 101 yards while the Packers ran five plays for 10 yards. Corum had 15 carries for 59 yards.
One of those carries came on a third-and-1 conversion. It was third-and-6 but the Packers were flagged for having 12 men on the field; the officials didn’t give Matt LaFleur the timeout. Then, on second-and-9 with Parsons on the field to rush the passer, Corum exploded up the middle for 12.
The defense escaped with a big third-down stop, so Love and the offense started at their 11 with 12:35 left in regulation. A 6-yard run by Kaleb Johnson was a promising start; a false start by Johnson was a setback. Love was almost intercepted on second-and-9 and Tucker Kraft couldn’t move the chain on a third-down screen.
With Corum storming up the middle for a gain of 35, the Rams extended their lead to 23-13 with 6:13 remaining in the game. Considering the Packers had zero first downs to that point of the second half and Christian Watson was out with a concussion, they faced long, long odds against Myles Garrett, Aaron Donald and the Rams’ juggernaut defense.
Those odds fell to basically zero when Love threw his second interception. It was Green Bay’s third turnover – the third time in four games they hit that dubious mark. One more field goal turned out to be the whipped cream on the pumpkin pie for the Rams.
The Packers got the ball to start the game but went three-and-out. The first play of the game was a completion to Christian Watson, but he limped off the field. Back-to-back incomplete passes led to a three-and-out.
With the Rams’ offense on the field, Micah Parsons got the start. He played the first three snaps but the Rams didn’t run anything his direction – a theme throughout the first half. A 39-yard penalty on Brandon Cisse – a bit of a ticky-tack flag – put the ball in scoring position, and Brandon McManus booted a 43-yard field goal.
The Packers approached midfield on the next drive, even though Kaleb Johnson lost 6 yards on two no-prayer carries. However, Tucker Kraft got the ball punched out by linebacker Nate Landman and nickel Quentin Lake recovered, giving the Rams the ball at their 43.
A roughing-the-passer penalty on Devonte Wyatt – the 10th this season by the Packers – gave the Rams 15 yards. The defense stiffened, though. Parsons’ pressure on Matthew Stafford produced a wayward pass and helped force McManus to kick a 41-yard field goal.
Green Bay answered with a 54-yard field goal by Trey Smack. Johnson lost 2 yards on the first play, but Watson had a 32-yard catch-and-run-and-hurdle on the next play. The drive died, though, when Kraft couldn’t hang onto a pass over the middle after he was hit by safety Kamren Kinchens.
The first quarter ended with Parsons having played nine snaps and getting the one pressure.
The Rams blew right through Green Bay’s defense to start the second quarter. After Stafford found Kyren Williams on third-and-4 just before he was hit by Parsons, Stafford connected with receiver Konata Mumpfield for 24 and tight end Tyler Higbee for 14 more. One play later, Williams strolled through an enormous hole for a 7-yard touchdown to make it 13-3. Karl Brooks, Anthony Campbell and Isaiah McDuffie were blocked with ease.
The Packers hadn’t given up three consecutive scoring drives to start a game all season. So, they were in an early trouble spot considering the power of the Rams’ pass rush and needing an answer.
And what an answer. First, it was a flea-flicker from Jordan Love to Savion Williams and back to Love, who ripped a bullet to a toe-dragging Christian Watson for 21. Then, Love ripped one to Matthew Golden, who cut back inside for a catch-and-run gain of 39 to the Rams’ 20. Finally, on third-and-goal at the 6, Love faced immediate pressure from Byron Young but stepped up and hit Watson for a touchdown to cut the margin to 13-10.
The Packers forced a three-and-out on the next drive, with the Rams throwing a give-up screen on third-and-11 rather than deal with Micah Parsons.
The Packers tied the game 13-13 with 1:50 left in the half to cap a wild drive.
First, on third-and-1, Savion Williams ran for 13 on a well-blocked run up the middle; he wasn’t touched by a defender until he was about 5 yards downfield. Kevin Zeitler, who finally made his first start at right guard, suffered an injured left ankle when Williams sprinted past him. Aaron Banks, a career-long left guard, entered at right guard and pancaked Braden Fiske on MarShawn Lloyd’s 10-yard run.
On fourth-and-1 – actually, they needed about 5 feet – Love floated one up to Watson. Watson was obliterated by Kamren Kinchens at the sideline and couldn’t hang onto the ball. Kinchens was flagged for unnecessary roughness and kicked out of the game but Matthew Golden was flagged for offense pass interference, so it was the most painful of offsetting penalties.
Watson was down for a few minutes before walking to the locker room. Down one of his top playmakers, coach Matt LaFleur reconsidered his fourth-down decision and sent on kicker Trey Smack, who kicked a 48-yard field goal to tie the game at 13 with 1:50 left in the half.
On first down, Parsons roared past left tackle Alaric Jackson for a sack. The crowd roared and Parsons exhorted them to crank up the decibels. The Rams waved the white flag of surrender, and the teams went into break with a tie score.
Love was 12-of-18 for 154 yards in the first half.

title: Showdown Against Rams Marks Debuts for Two Potential Packers Saviors
full_text:
Almost two months after he was signed, guard Kevin Zeitler will make his long-awaited debut in the starting lineup for the Green Bay Packers against the Los Angeles Rams on Wednesday night at SoFi Stadium.
Zeitler was part of Green Bay’s No. 1 line during warmups. The starting line consisted of Jordan Morgan at left guard, Laken Tomlinson at left guard, Sean Rhyan at center, Zeitler at right guard and Anthony Belton at right tackle.
Rhyan is back in the lineup after missing the last three games. Zeitler will be making the 214th start of his career and his first since Jan. 4 while with the Titans.
The challenge could hardly be any tougher. The Rams probably have the best defensive line in the NFL. In their base defense, Myles Garrett and Byron Young are the edges and Aaron Donald, Kobie Turner and Braden Fiske.
“It’s a pretty legendary group over there,” Zeitler said this week.
Donald, an eight-time All-Pro, came out of retirement to chase a Super Bowl ring.
“A couple of times definitely over the years, [and it’s] absolutely stress-inducing every single time,” Zeitler said of Donald. “The guy’s a monster – always has been, always will be as long as he’s out on that field. It will take every single thing we’ve got as a team and as individuals to get it done.”
The Packers need their line to play its best game of the season against the Rams’ potent front. This will be their seventh starting combination of the year. Zeitler is the fourth player to start at right guard this year.
Green Bay gave up eight sacks last week. It enters Week 12 ranked last in the league in rushing, as well.
“The only thing we can do is do it out on the field,” Zeitler said. “It wasn’t pretty last week. I don’t think anyone can say otherwise. I think everyone’s acknowledged it in our room. We’ve got to turn it around. The only thing that matters is things changing on the field. We can talk all we want, but nothing matters until it changes and gets done.”
“It just has to happen. It’s as simple as that,” Zeitler said. “We work hard. We’re prepped well here. For whatever reason, things have not been going our way. Whatever that line is we have to cross, we have to get it crossed and get it done.”
☝️ pic.twitter.com/ldmpMYscA0
Micah Parsons, as expected, is active.
After 49 weeks away from the game, what will his emotions be like before the game?
“I would say I’m always pretty nervous before a game,” he said on Monday. “I’ll just be ready for the first snap. I’m just trying to stay right here with it. Not even look forward to that moment. Just enjoy every process, even leading up to the start of the snap. I’ll probably have some emotions after the game, but from what I hear from family, I’m not really big on emotions.”
Parsons went through three weeks of practice to put the finishing touches on his comeback. He went through pregame warmups without a brace on his knee.
His goal for the next seven games has nothing to do with individual stats and accolades.
“I would say I have no targets,” he said. “The only thing I’m targeting in a sense of mindset is to win every week to try to up lift this season, change this season around, and do exactly what the Packers brought me here to do. That’s it. That’s my only target and that’s to make a run for the playoffs and make guys around me better. That’s it.
“I think talking to a friend of mine who went through the ACL process, we were talking about it like, we push and we ignore so many other things that’s wrong with this because we’re always chasing the outcome and we just keep chasing the outcomes, whether it’s the All-Pros or the Pro Bowls and when you end up injured none of that stuff actually matters anymore. Everyone’s like, ‘Oh, well, when will he be back?’ And we chase these things for so long that those outcomes become dust and people don’t really care about that. It’s about what you can do next or can you do it again? So, I have no targets and outcomes.”
Well, there is one target. The Packers brought him to Green Bay to help win a Super Bowl. Parsons, whose record streak of five consecutive seasons of 12-plus sacks to open his career almost certainly will be snapped, wants to make that a reality.
“I think I’ve achieved everything that I’ve wanted in my career except for the big one and I think that’s kind of like my own mindset,” he continued. “Through the Saban documentary, I learned just stay in the process of every day. Own my process my today, so I owned it today. I got another process tomorrow and God willing, I’ll have another process Wednesday night and that’ll be the start of this new journey.”
The inactives for today's Week 12 game against the Rams
Two starters, running back Josh Jacobs and linebacker Zaire Franklin, are inactive.
Both players practiced all week and were questionable. Coach Matt LaFleur didn’t think Jacobs would play, and that was the case. Franklin, meanwhile, returned to practice this week but will miss a fourth consecutive game.
Isaiah McDuffie and Ty’Ron Hopper will start against the Rams’ potent running game.
“I feel like they did great,” Franklin said. “It’s always a blessing to be surrounded by a lot of talent. I did my best to continue to support the guys in any way that I could, whether that’s energy on the sideline or notes in the meetings or helping coach up on the sideline. But there’s only so much you can do when you’re not on the field. So, just looking forward to being who I’m supposed to be on the field.”

title: Steelers Bench and Release Aaron Rodgers; Should Packers Sign Him?
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – Thanksgiving Eve was supposed to be about the Green Bay Packers and Los Angeles Rams.
Instead, the men who led the Packers to their last Super Bowl win, Mike McCarthy and Aaron Rodgers, stole the turkey and pumpkin pie.
And the ice cream sandwiches. And then took a snore-filled snooze.
The Steelers on Tuesday night announced that they had benched Rodgers – Rodgers allegedly learned the news from teammate Pat Freiermuth. Rodgers, naturally, went on The Pat McAfee Show to go scorched earth on McCarthy, accusing him of napping in team meetings and skipping walk-throughs.
The Steelers, predictably, Rodgers released shortly thereafter.
It’s possible Rodgers’ NFL career is over. He had said this would be his final season, anyway, and now he’s out of a job. The bad teams have no need to bring in Rodgers as a starting quarterback. The good teams might not want to upset the apple cart by bringing in Rodgers as a backup quarterback.
However, what about the team for which he won four NFL MVPs?
The Packers are 6-4 entering Wednesday night’s game at the Rams. A win over Los Angeles would be a key step – and necessary step – toward returning the playoffs for a fourth consecutive year since the Packers traded Rodgers to the Jets in 2023.
The Packers are a good team with a really good quarterback. Jordan Love has been the rising tide that lifts all boats. He’s led a team with a horrendous offensive line, no running game and an abundance of dropped passes and penalties into position to reach the playoffs.
But there is no margin for error. If Love were to be knocked out for two quarters of a game or for two games, the Packers would face an almost insurmountable challenge to win. And given their backs-against-the-wall spot in the playoff race, their postseason hopes could be knocked out if Love were to be knocked out of a game.
The Packers enjoyed two years of sensational backup play with Malik Willis. With Willis signing to become the starting quarterback with the Dolphins this past offseason, the Packers pivoted to 37-year-old Tyrod Taylor. Taylor has had a long and successful career, but his best days are, clearly, behind him. His value to the roster is in his experience, wisdom and know-how.
Taylor is probably good enough to keep the Packers in the game against lesser opponents but he’s probably not good enough to go out and win a game against a quality opponent – and there’s a bunch of those on Green Bay’s remaining schedule.
Rodgers will turn 43 next week. He, obviously, isn’t the player who won Super Bowl MVP in 2010 and NFL MVPs in 2011, 2014, 2020 and 2021. He’s not the player who ranks fourth in NFL history in passer rating.
But he’s not bad – and would be an upgrade over Taylor. He had three consecutive games of three touchdown passes for the Steelers earlier this season. He’s immobile and no longer a magician in the pocket. But he can still sling the football and can win any play before the ball is snapped.
If Love were to miss a game or two, who would give the Packers the better chance of winning a game and keeping their season alive? Taylor or Rodgers.
Yes, there is baggage. That is obvious. Rodgers threw McCarthy under the bus in Green Bay and, predictably, did it again during their reunion season in Pittsburgh.
One high-ranking executive told Packers On SI that he wouldn’t touch Rodgers with a “1,000-foot pole.”
But if you’re general manager Brian Gutekunst and the goal is to build the best top-to-bottom roster to weather whatever challenge comes your way, then adding Rodgers should at least be a conversation.
The conversation would have to start internally with coach Matt LaFleur. LaFleur and Rodgers butted heads during their four seasons together, but they also reached incredible heights. From a team perspective, there were trips to the NFC Championship Game in 2019 and 2020 and the No. 1 seed in 2021. From a personal perspective, Rodgers won MVP in 2020 and 2021.
The conversation, obviously, would have to include Love. By all accounts, including their own, they enjoyed a strong relationship during their three seasons together. When the Packers traded Rodgers, Rodgers understood that Love’s time had arrived. What would Love think about sharing a quarterback room with Rodgers again?
And then there would have to be a long and brutally honest conversation with Rodgers.
What would Rodgers think about a full-circle ending to his career? From 2015 through 2017, Rodgers was the backup to Brett Favre. Now, he’d be the backup to Love for the final handful of games of his final season.
What would Rodgers think about being the clear and obvious backup quarterback? There would be no scenario in which Rodgers would compete for the starting job or push for playing time. He’d be the football equivalent of a fire extinguisher, with the glass broken only in case of emergency.
Would Rodgers be a distraction? Not if handled correctly by all parties. Other than talking to reporters upon joining the Packers, he would not make himself available to media. He would not go on the air with McAfee. He wouldn’t say a word. He’d be as anonymous as the backup long snapper during training camp.
Yes, he’d be a hot topic for a few days but, so long as Rodgers embraced the role of being one of 53 players on the roster – nothing more, nothing less – the story would quickly die down.
Rodgers remains a good quarterback. Not a great quarterback but he’s a good one. He could help the Packers if disaster struck on gameday. He could help Love behind the scenes because of his experience in 267 career starts and in LaFleur’s offense.
Love has taken a beating at times this season behind Green Bay’s undermanned and/or underprepared offensive line. Maybe Love can survive all 17-plus games and play every meaningful snap. He’s also one blown block away from the sideline.
While there’s a narrative that Rodgers is a selfish, uncoachable, back-stabber, he loved his time in Green Bay and holds the team in high regard. Chances are, he’d be a model citizen.
“The falls there are just awesome, when the weather gets that cool little nip,” he said before the Packers-Steelers preseason game. “I loved the night games at Lambeau, especially the Sunday nights, Monday nights and occasional Thursday nights. Just so much fun. There’s nothing like that crowd. Been other places, but there’s nothing like that fan base and the way they travel and the crowds at home.
“Players around the league they talk about how special it is to play at Lambeau, and sometimes you might miss that or forget about that when you’re playing because it becomes so normal to have such an amazing crowd and they’re tailgating and they’re loud and they rarely sell their tickets to other teams’ fans.
“There’s a lot of great things about Wisconsin. I grew up there, really, and became a little more mature as an adult over the years there and had a great time and still have a lot of close friends there, a lot of fond memories.”
Or, as Rodgers said in his good-bye to Green Bay after the trade “This is not the end for us. I will see you again Green Bay, you’ll always have my heart.”
Rodgers spent 18 glorious seasons with the Packers. If everyone is in the right spot mentally – and that is a big if, obviously – he could finish his career where it started.

title: Packers-Rams Predictions: Who Will Win Showdown 32,200 Days in the Making?
full_text:
The Green Bay Packers have played only one Wednesday game in franchise history, a 24-22 win over the Chicago Cardinals in Buffalo in 1938. That was 32,200 days ago.
“Obviously, this is a unique thing. The NFL made up their own holiday,” linebacker Zaire Franklin said. “I’ll be looking forward to celebrating the new holiday, Thanksgiving Eve, with all you guys in LA. So, that’ll be pretty fun.”
It’s a huge game. Both teams are 6-4. The winner will remain in the lead for the final spot in the NFC playoffs. The loser will essentially be two games behind because of the tiebreaker.
“Man, there’s nothing worse than losing off the bye. Hate it,” Franklin said. “And I don’t like losing with a long plane ride. So, triple reasons to get the win.”
Even with their injury issues on offense , the Rams are 2.5-point favorites at FanDuel Sportsbook; the line had been 3. Who will earn the crucial victory? Here are our weekly game predictions.
The Rams were the overwhelming favorites to win this year’s Super Bowl before the season. They overhauled their defense by adding legendary edge rusher Myles Garrett and cornerbacks Trent McDuffie and Jaylen Watson. Enticed by their potential, legendary defensive tackle Aaron Donald came out of retirement.
Games are played on the field and not on paper. The Rams started 2-4, including a woeful home loss to the Cardinals. However, they’ve rounded into form with four consecutive wins. They’ve allowed just 28 points the last three games, with Garrett recording three sacks against the Commanders and Donald 1.5 sacks in the rematch against the Cardinals.
Last week, Packers quarterback Jordan Love was pummeled for eight sacks in about two-and-a-half quarters. If they couldn’t block the Vikings, how on earth are they going to block Garrett, Donald, Byron Young and Kobie Turner? They are the best four-man rush in the league.
It sounds like Mission Impossible, with the potential of Love getting the stuffing knocked out of him for a second consecutive week.
However, the Packers’ defense will get a major lift with the return of Micah Parsons. The question entering the season was whether the defense could survive the first four-or-so games of the season without Parsons. Well, it survived the first 10 games.
While the Packers are in relatively good health, the Rams will be limping into the game. Premier receiver Puka Nacua is on injured reserve with a knee injury and Davante Adams remains on IR with a hamstring injury. Plus, their starting left guard and starting center will be inactive. Added together, there is a real opportunity for Green Bay’s defense to feast.
On the other side of the ball, the Rams’ pass rush is going to create all sorts of problems, though the return of center Sean Rhyan and the potential starting debut of right guard Kevin Zeitler should help. They’ll have to be studs so the Packers can swing the pressure toward whoever has to deal with Garrett.
Regardless of who’s blocking, coach Matt LaFleur and quarterback Jordan Love had better have learned a lesson from last week. LaFleur needs to call some quick-hitting passes and Love needs to run those quick-hitting passes rather than sticking with his bombs-away mentality. McDuffie is having a sensational season but Watson is on injured reserve, so there should be some opportunities for receivers Christian Watson and Matthew Golden.
Ultimately, the bigger advantage is with Green Bay’s defense against Los Angeles’ beat-up offense. Parsons, Xavier McKinney and Evan Williams will make enough plays to give the Packers the victory necessary to propel them toward a run to the playoffs.
Who’s getting the W tomorrow? 🤔 pic.twitter.com/bUX4vDaSlY
Bill’s Prediction: Packers 20, Rams 17.
This is a tough matchup for Green Bay.
The Rams’ defense is excellent against the run, so the Packers’ putrid run game will have even less room to roam than usual.
The passing game is going to struggle with Myles Garrett and Aaron Donald breathing down Jordan Love’s neck for most of the night. Once the ball does go in the air, Trent McDuffie is one of the best cornerbacks in football. He could take away one of Green Bay’s top two passing options.
So, why take the Packers? The return of Micah Parsons should give the defense an emotional boost. That doesn’t even include what he could be on the field. Green Bay’s defense has been good without Parsons this year. With him back, if he is even close to his usual, dominant self, they have the ceiling to be one of the best defenses in football.
After suffering knee injuries in Week 15 of last season, Micah Parsons is expected to make his return vs Rams in Week 12 😤 pic.twitter.com/pVqnMsTxQJ
Couple that fact with the fact Matthew Stafford will be missing his top two receivers and two starters on the offensive line.
This game could come down to one game-changing turnover. If we’re calling our shot, we’ll bet on Parsons stripping Stafford to set up a game-winning drive for Love.
Jacob’s Prediction: Packers 21, Rams 17.

title: Three Fear Factors Why Rams Will Sack Packers in Pivotal Thanksgiving Eve Showdown
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – It’s not a must-win game but it’s pretty darned close.
The Green Bay Packers are 6-4 and clinging to the final playoff spot in the NFC. The Los Angeles Rams – the preseason Super Bowl favorites – are 6-4 and right on their heels. The winner of Wednesday’s made-up holiday showdown will not only have a one-game lead over the loser but also own the tiebreaker.
Here are three reasons why the Packers will lose to the Rams and see their playoff teetering on thin ice.
Games aren’t won on first down and they’re not decided between the 20s.
No, games are decided on third down and in the red zone. In all four areas, the Rams have enormous advantages.
When the Packers have the ball, they are 20th on third down (37.2 percent conversions) and 20th in the red zone (54.3 percent touchdowns). On defense, the Rams are second on third down (30.0 percent conversions) and fourth in the red zone (43.3 percent touchdowns).
“It’s a really sound defense, obviously,” Packers coach Matt LaFleur said when asked about the Rams in those areas. “They’ve got some creatures up front that are a problem. I think they do a great job in the back end. It’s well coordinated just in terms of challenging when they play man, and then when they’re playing their soft zones, of not getting beat deep and giving stuff over the top.
“I think all in all, I just don’t see many holes and there’s not many weaknesses to the defense. I think Chris Shula does an unbelievable job coordinating  that thing and putting those guys in position to be playmakers, and then they have playmakers.”
When the Packers are on defense, they are 22nd on third down (42.7 percent conversions) and 21st in the red zone (63.6 percent touchdowns). The Rams are ninth on third down (41.8 percent conversions) and seventh in the red zone (66.7 percent touchdowns).
To put a bow on it, in all four categories, the Packers are 20th or worse and the Rams are inside the top 10.
In what's essentially a must-win game, here are three reasons why the Packers will earn a critical victory over the Rams tonight. (Opposite side of this story coming shortly.) ⬇️ https://t.co/t25ekTvQDE
Obviously, the matchup will not be Packers running back Kaleb Johnson vs. Rams running back Kyren Williams. But the Rams have an elite rushing attack, meaning they can mitigate the Packers’ pass rush, and the Packers have a putrid rushing attack, meaning the Rams can attack Jordan Love with little fear.
Los Angeles enters the game ranked seventh in rushing yards per game (133.0) and per carry (4.62). It has an outside chance of having two 1,000-yard rushers with Williams (616 yards, 4.4 average and six touchdowns) and Blake Corum (547 yards, 5.3 average, five touchdowns). Both rank among the top 20 individuals in rushing yards.
Williams is the proven workhorse with three consecutive seasons of 1,100-plus rushing yards and double-digits touchdowns, but Corum is the hot hand as he comes off a 100-yard game at Arizona and is on a streak of four consecutive games with a touchdown.
“Yeah, you can’t tackle them,” defensive coordinator Jonathan Gannon said. “That’s what they’ve shown. They’ve got really good contact balance. They’re both very strong, they’ve got really good vision, they’ve got good patience with their run scheme. I think what goes unnoticed is how they make it go with the acceleration when they need the acceleration, the hesitation when they need the hesitation to let the blocks declare.
“I’ve got a high opinion of both of these guys. And they’re both weapons out of the backfield, so they can hurt you in the pass game, as well. I’m not screens; I’m talking out on routes as receivers. They’ve got really good players in a really good scheme and it’s another reason they put a lot of points on a lot of people.”
Aside from the one horrendous game against the Falcons, Green Bay’s run defense has been solid this season, though it has allowed the fourth-most rushing touchdowns (12) in the league.
The run offense is another story. The Packers are last in the league with 67.0 rushing yards per game and 3.06 yards per carry. Johnson has provided a bit of a spark but can he do enough against a Rams run defense that ranks 11th with 3.92 yards allowed per carry to give the offense necessary balance?
“We have that mindset every week to go out there and try to dominate,” Rams defensive tackle Aaron Donald told reporters this week. “We have to go out there and do it, starting with stopping the run. We have to be able to play the run well and get them in situations where they have to pass. If we do that, we feel like we can take advantage, but we have to earn that.”
The Packers are going to be in big trouble, and Jordan Love is going to be in a world of hurt, if it becomes a pass-every-play kind of game.
The Rams will be wearing throwback jerseys to the Fearsome Foursome era. These Rams have a fearsome pass rush.
In his first game back following a two-month layoff, outside linebacker Myles Garrett had three sacks. Defensive tackle Aaron Donald, who came out of retirement to chase a Super Bowl ring, had 1.5 sacks last week. Defensive tackle Kobie Turner, who had nine sacks as a rookie alongside Donald in 2023, eight in 2024 and seven in 2025, was activated from injured reserve this week. Outside linebacker Byron Young has 5.5 sacks this season after a career-high 12 last year.
Along with defensive tackle Braden Fiske, the Rams have five players who can get after the quarterback.
“The front. That’s what stands out to you,” Love said. “Obviously, Myles Garrett, Aaron Donald, they’ve got a lot of good guys up front. Especially when they’re in base, you get five one-on-one blocks. They’ve got some good players over there, so that definitely stands out.
“It’s something that we talk about it all week, it starts up front. We’ve got to handle business. We’ve got to be able to block the front, give me some time and in the run game, we’ve got to be able to get hands on people, create some lanes in the run game. But I think if you look at their team, the defensive front stands out.”
With the Browns, Garrett set an NFL record with 23 sacks last season and led the league with 33 tackles for losses, including a half-sack and four pressures against the Packers.
“There’s not too many guys with his size and speed,” coach Matt LaFleur said. “He’s got a great get-off. Obviously, his strength is as good as anybody. It’s a rare combo of size and speed.”
Green Bay allowed eight sacks last week against the Vikings. The challenge won’t be schematic this week; the Rams are only 18th in blitz rate. The challenge will be winning the individual matchups because they can’t double team everyone.
“They try to press and assert their will, and they’re looking for a game to break through that barrier, and we can’t allow that to be us,” Garrett said. “They have an exceptional quarterback in Jordan Love, who can push the ball downfield and make plays, which they’ve done pretty much all season to this point.
“We can’t allow them to be versatile with being able to [rush] on the ground and gain yards there but also push down the field with his arm. We’re going to have to make them one-dimensional and get after the passer.”
It's been almost exactly 10 years since Aaron Rodgers said the Packers could run the table. And they did. Maybe this year's team can run the table, too. @JacobWestendorf looks at why the Packers can win their final games. https://t.co/Adx3g95lTj

title: Texans Get Marvin Harrison Jr. Back, But WR Injury Woes Continue
full_text:
The Houston Texans were able to see one of their recently injured wide receivers take a step towards suiting up once again in Week 12 against the Baltimore Ravens.
That's because Marvin Harrison Jr.–– who has missed the last two games due to a lingering hamstring injury–– was finally able to practice in limited capacity during Houston's Wednesday practice session .
It's the first time that Harrison Jr. has participated with the team in any capacity since November 12th, when he presumably suffered the hamstring injury in practice.
That led to an absence against the Cleveland Browns and Indianapolis Colts, and thus, a shorthanded Texans wide receiver room. But with increased participation over the next two sessions, there's a good chance that Harrison Jr. will be good to go against Baltimore.
However, the Texans' wide receiver injuries still managed to linger into their Wednesday practice, despite Harrison Jr.'s individual status trending in the right direction.
That's because Kayshon Boutte was a DNP during practice with a hip injury he suffered during last week's game against the Colts.
Boutte's DNP is eye-catching. Not only because the wide receiver wound up missing practice, but also for the fact that it came even after the Texans' extended mini-bye that came as a result of their last game being played on Thursday.
And the injury for Boutte unfortunately comes fresh off of Boutte's strongest game in a while.
Against the Colts, Boutte hauled in both of his targets for two receptions and 40 yards, also bringing in a big-time touchdown grab in the second quarter for C.J. Stroud's second of three scores on the day.
It marked Boutte's second game of the season in which he's had 40 or more reception yards, and his third touchdown reception on the year as well.
Boutte still has two days to potentially practice, and thus see his status for Sunday against Baltimore to trend in the right direction. But if he's unable to participate on Thursday, there's an increasingly likely chance that Houston will be down yet another receiver due to injury.
Despite the Texans having what's been viewed as a deep receiving room at many times this season, they haven't had a ton of opportunities to show off this entire unit in its full capacity, simply due to ongoing injury issues at the position.
Jayden Higgins was viewed as an emerging WR2 in the Texans' passing attack, then tore his ACL before the first game . Jaylin Noel just caught fire through the first half of the season, then had a season-ending toe injury.
Nico Collins has missed a couple of games with a hamstring injury. Marvin Harrison Jr. has missed two appearances since his arrival, also with a hamstring injury. Tank Dell just got back in Week 7 from his own knee injury. Now, Kayshon Boutte is dealing with his hip issue. You get the point.
Thankfully, thanks to that extensive depth at the position, the Texans will have a healthy-enough unit to roll into Week 12's game against Baltimore and still have a potent arsenal for Stroud to work with.
Collins, Dell, potentially Harrison Jr., and Xavier Hutchinson will all be good to go, and each of those guys has shown their respective flashes of production over the course of this season.
Yet, another wide receiver injury–– this time to Boutte–– just goes to show how beaten up Houston has been at the position all season long.

title: 3 Things the Texans Should Be Thankful for This Thanksgiving
full_text:
The Houston Texans have a lot to be thankful for this holiday season.
For one, they don't have to play their Week 12 game until Sunday , unlike 10 of the other teams currently participating in games from Wednesday through Friday––giving the roster a bit more rest and time with their families before a pivotal matchup against the Baltimore Ravens.
But outside of those implications, there's even more for the Texans to have gratitude for.
While the first half of this season hasn't gone exactly how anyone in the building has intended, hope is still alive to turn things around in the second half of the year. And with momentum seemingly coming at the right time, there might be even more for this group to be thankful for by the time we hit New Year's.
But for now, as Thanksgiving approaches, as does the home stretch for the NFL season with just seven games to go, let's break down three key things the Texans should be most thankful for:
It's funny how things work. It was less than 12 months ago where many fans and national media members were questioning C.J. Stroud's ability to be the Texans' long-term guy under center after a less-than-ideal playoff loss.
But after the first 11 games of this season, Stroud has left no doubts about his ability to be an elite-level quarterback in the NFL, as he's performed as one of the best at his position throughout most of the year––to the point where it's not too outlandish to consider him a dark horse MVP candidate.
He probably won't end up winning it, simply due to the sluggish start the Texans had to this season that currently puts them on the outside looking in for the postseason, but Stroud's individual production can't be overlooked.
He's on pace to record over 4,500 passing yards and over 35 passing touchdowns, which should be a leap that the Texans are more than thankful for. They'll get their chance to show their gratitude in the form of a lucrative contract extension later this offseason.
The Texans' defense hasn't been as consistently elite as they proved to be throughout last season. Their run defense has been solid, but has had its moments. The secondary has been prone to giving up big plays. The linebacker unit has been battered with injuries all season long.
But throughout all of the chaos the Texans have had on their defense, one presence has remained just as dominant, if not even more so, from where he stood last year–– and that's current Defensive Player of the Year frontrunner Will Anderson Jr.
Anderson has been a wrecking ball on the Texans' defensive line that has stamped him atop the NFL leaderboards for sacks (11.5), total pressures (60), and pressure rate (19.3%).
He's stepped up in the time that Danielle Hunter has been out with a lingering hamstring injury, so much so that he came away with the AFC's Defensive Player of the Week after his Week 11 performance against the Indianapolis Colts.
Without Anderson, who knows where the Texans' defense would rank right now? Thankfully, Houston doesn't have to worry. And if he keeps up this pace, his efforts should be rewarded at the end of the season with some new hardware for his trophy case and a second-straight All-Pro nod.
Somehow, the Texans are still right within the hunt of clawing their way into the postseason despite falling to an 0-4 record to initially start the season.
And based on how some of the surrounding teams in the AFC are trending (i.e. the Pittsburgh Steelers, Baltimore Ravens), Houston should be feeling more and more optimistic about their chances of a fourth straight postseason appearance every passing week.
Houston wasn't supposed to be here. After the Texans had dropped their first four games––and even after losses in Weeks 7 and 10 in very winnable games––many had written off this team and their chances of a late postseason run.
But as we stand with seven weeks to go, they're only two games back from positioning themselves as the seventh seed. And their next two games are against a couple of AFC threats right within the hunt as well.
It would make for the most miraculous feat we've seen in DeMeco Ryans' tenure as the Texans' head coach; coming back from 0-4 to be the second team in NFL history to make the postseason. But if Houston can keep the hot hand for the next few games, a playoff bid is very much possible.

title: Texans Injury Report: 5 Players Miss Practice Ahead of Ravens Matchup
full_text:
The Houston Texans have released their first injury report of the week rolling into their Week 12 matchup against the Baltimore Ravens .
And on the status for some players, things seem to be trending in the right direction. In the case of five others, they wound up not practicing on Wednesday, and thus makes their status a bit more cloudy as it relates to this weekend's action.
Let's break down the latest on the injury front from the Texans' practice a few days away from the Ravens traveling to Reliant Stadium:
TE Brevin Jordan (finger/foot) WR Kayshon Boutte (hip) DE Danielle Hunter (hamstring) OL Keylan Rutledge (neck/shoulder) DT Sheldon Rankins (ankle)
WR Marvin Harrison Jr. (hamstring) LB Jake Hummel (abdomen/groin) DE Logan Hall (hip/shoulder)
CB Kamari Lassiter (wrist) RB Woody Marks (concussion) S Reed Blankenship (hand) LB Jake Hansen (elbow) OT Blake Fisher (thumb) OT Trent Brown (wrist)
Let's break down some of the good news first: two of the Texans' bigger names on the offensive end that missed last week's game against the Colts managed to practice on Wednesday: that's running back Woody Marks (concussion) and wide receiver Marvin Harrison Jr. (hamstring)
With two more days of practice to go for each, there's a good chance that both guys will be able to suit up against the Ravens considering everything continues to move in the right direction.
DeMeco Ryans noted that the team was "hopeful" Marks would make his return earlier this week, and signs appear to be pointing in that direction. Marks will pair up next to David Montgomery within the Texans' backfield, who came off a game where he posted his season-high in rushing yards with 107.
As for those that the Texans are at risk of being without on Sunday, though, there's a couple of names on each side of the ball to watch out for.
Most notably, defensive end Danielle Hunter still isn't practicing yet after suffering his hamstring injury before Week 10's game against the Cleveland Browns .
Houston will likely have to see Hunter practice once ahead of this coming weekend to have optimism around his playing status against Baltimore, but the team could be taking a rather cautious approach around one of their older, more impactful veterans on the defense.
Another older veteran on the Texans defense— defensive end Sheldon Rankins— also didn't practice on Wednesday.
Being without Hunter is enough of a challenge for Houston to overcome, but losing their top defensive tackle in Rankins could make things even tougher, if he is inevitably ruled out for this weekend. He's got two more days to practice and change the feelings around his status.
Offensively, the Texans had some concerns worth noting as well: wide receiver Kayshon Boutte is still dealing with the effects from his hip injury sustained on Thursday Night Football, and could put his status to play this weekend in doubt.
If Boutte is out, the Texans' wide receiver room will continue to look thin, as it has been since moving past the bye; relying on only Nico Collins, Tank Dell, Xavier Hutchinson, and Marvin Harrison Jr., if he continues to trend in the right direction.
Keylan Rutledge is also still dealing with some of the effects of his injury suffered last week against the Colts, which turned out to be his second stinger of the year in the second half.
If Rutledge is set to miss any time moving forward, expect the Texans to roll with Febechi Nwaiwu as their fill-in at left guard. However, still with two more days of practice to go, there's still room for his and everyone else's status to improve between now and game day.

title: Texans, C.J. Stroud Among Biggest Winners of Steelers-Rodgers Drama
full_text:
The Pittsburgh Steelers made an eye-catching, and really, a stunning change to their offense heading into Week 12 of the NFL season.
After having Aaron Rodgers under center as their starting quarterback for the last 26 consecutive games, the Steelers have decided to bench the future Hall of Famer for Mason Rudolph for their upcoming game vs. the Denver Broncos, leaving Rodgers as an inactive on their gameday roster.
pic.twitter.com/F2qo4OawcY
The change in the Steelers' quarterback room is one that was largely unpredictable.
Rodgers was all but locked into his spot as Pittsburgh's QB1, despite their lackluster passing production across the first half of the season, and after their latest 16-19 loss to the Philadelphia Eagles, he might've finally played his last game in the NFL with no signs that Pittsburgh plans on turning to him moving forward.
However, as the Steelers have made a big change under center, there's a chance that the Texans and C.J. Stroud now come out of this decision as some of the biggest winners of all––and that's for more reasons than one.
One of the most important fallouts from this decision that connects with the Texans is the fact that Houston will be playing this same Steelers team in a little over a week come Week 13's Sunday Night Football matchup; a game that could have significant consequences for playoff seeding in the AFC.
The Texans have a history of taking care of Rodgers and the Steelers' offense as of their most recent matchup in the Wild Card Round of last postseason, where Houston claimed a dominant 30-6 victory on the road at Acrisure Stadium.
But for their matchup against the Steelers looming this season, they'll now be faced with the task of seeing Mason Rudolph, which could be a simpler–– or perhaps even tougher battle for the Texans to take on–– depending on how Rudolph looks as Pittsburgh's QB1 on Friday against Denver.
On top of the implications now in play for the Texans' Week 13 game, the AFC Wild Card race now has a bunch of backup-level quarterbacks competing alongside Houston that now tend to make their road to the postseason suddenly a bit more palatable.
Of the six teams that are reasonably within the hunt to make some noise in the postseason, only two of those teams have yet to make a significant change at the quarterback position: that's the Texans, who have C.J. Stroud playing at an MVP-level , and the Cleveland Browns with Deshaun Watson.
Current starting QBs of the six AFC teams I believe will fight for the last two playoff spots … • Browns: Deshaun Watson • Steelers: Mason Rudolph • Patriots: Tommy DeVito • Texans: CJ Stroud • Raiders: Fernando Mendoza • Ravens: Jacoby Brissett Advantage: Houston.
Having the edge at quarterback can be a much-welcomed lift for any NFL team on a given week, but that's especially so for those looking to make a run into the playoffs.
The top five teams sitting clearly above the Texans in the AFC standings each have an above-average to elite option at quarterback: the Buffalo Bills and Josh Allen, the Denver Broncos and Bo Nix, the Jacksonville Jaguars and Trevor Lawrence, the Cincinnati Bengals and Joe Burrow, and the Kansas City Chiefs and Patrick Mahomes.
The Texans and Stroud aren't far away from becoming that sixth or seventh team in the standings. With a few victories in a row over the next few weeks against winnable matchups like the Ravens and Steelers, along with the Philadelphia Eagles and Tennessee Titans, it might be just enough to give Houston the necessary lift in the Wild Card race .
And if that late-season run does come to form again for the Texans, that only helps Stroud and his case of cashing in an even bigger check once it comes time to negotiate a new contract extension later this offseason.
But making such a run happen all starts with the Texans taking care of business against the Ravens, then doing so once again against the Steelers the following week, which would then lift Houston to .500 for the first time this season.
With Pittsburgh's latest decision to turn away from a Hall of Fame quarterback like Rodgers until further notice, those chances of the Texans making that climb happen begin to look a whole lot better.

title: Predicting Texans' Final 7 Games as Playoff Hopes Remain Alive
full_text:
The Houston Texans are creeping closer and closer to being within range of a playoff spot in the AFC , as they sit at 4-6 with just seven games to go on the schedule, but ride into those upcoming matchups with some positive momentum on their side.
So how could those upcoming games for the Texans pan out? They've got three matchups at home and four on the road, and each of them are looking critical for their chances of clawing their way up the AFC ladder for a top-seven seed.
With that in mind, let's take a look at all seven matchups that are on the horizon for the Texans, predict how each could go, and see how their record pans out at the end.
The Ravens are on a six-game losing streak, are still without Lamar Jackson, and are taking the road against a Texans team with some momentum building up in their favor.
While the Ravens did play the Carolina Panthers close this past weekend, Houston's scoring attack combined with their improving defense should overwhelm them enough for the Texans to win back-to-back home games for the first time since 2025.
Prediction: Texans Win, 31-13
The Texans get a chance to face the Steelers in a primetime setting for the second time this calendar year on Sunday Night Football. And while Pittsburgh's defense could cause some distress for C.J. Stroud, it's hard to imagine their offense making much of a dent on the other end.
That's especially so after the Steelers just announced they were benching Aaron Rodgers in Week 12 for Mason Rudolph. This is a game the Texans have to take advantage of, and should, which would finally take them to .500 for the first time this year–– so long as they take care of Baltimore.
Prediction: Texans Win, 28-10
This is a sneaky game for the Texans that could quickly become a challenging one by the time we get to Week 14.
Washington is currently on a two-game win streak that could quickly turn to four with wins over the Arizona Cardinals and Tennessee Titans, and could lead to Jayden Daniels and Co. being a bit of a freight train to stop, especially on their home field.
However, the Texans would be a pretty tough force to stop at this point as well. They'd be on a three-game win streak, and if their defense is catching fire, Jayden Daniels and the Commanders’ offensive line might be overwhelmed enough for Houston to keep things rolling for a much-needed Week 14 win.
Prediction: Texans Win, 23-21
This is undoubtedly the toughest game left on the Texans' schedule; a rematch against a divisional opponent in which they already beat once this season. But it's even harder to beat a team twice in a season––and for a Super Bowl contender like Jacksonville, they could be best equipped to stop Houston on a hypothetical win streak.
Perhaps the Texans gut out a last-minute victory in their second game of the season against Jacksonville, as they did around this time last year. However, I've got Jacksonville and their improved roster from Week 6's meeting splitting their season series vs. Houston, and paving the way to an inevitable AFC South victory.
Prediction: Texans Lose, 17-16
This needs to be a game the Texans come out with a win in. The Eagles have sunken to the bottom of the NFC North, will likely be starting Joe Milton, and might just be gunning towards better draft positioning at this point in the year, rather than playing spoiler to Houston's playoff hopes.
The Eagles do lead the all-time series against the Texans 6-0. So maybe claiming a win here will be easier said than done. But their offense appears to have no chance of overcoming what could be a dangerous Houston defense at this point in the year, and could lead to a resounding road victory.
Prediction: Texans Win, 21-6
This is another challenge for the Texans that might be a bit too tough to overcome: a road test against a fiery offense in another playoff threat, the Packers, who could have their defense rolling for their best production of the season with Micah Parsons back in the lineup.
Maybe the Texans will be able to defy historical precedent in this game once again. Green Bay is 5-1 all-time against Houston. But it seems like it would have to take some real C.J. Stroud heroics or a star-studded Will Anderson to take down the Packers here. I'll have them coming up just short by less than a touchdown.
Prediction: Texans Lose, 23-17
This is the perfect moment for a cathartic win over a division rival they've already bested once this season. While the Titans will certainly be playing for pride in their final game of the year, Houston will be searching for any life that might be left for a playoff appearance and end the regular season off with a home victory.
The Texans have already dominated the Titans for a 20-plus point victory in October, and the same could be in store once Week 18 rolls around.
Prediction: Texans Win, 33-6
If each of these seven projections pans out, the Texans end up at 9-8. Not exactly eliminated from the postseason picture, but they'd certainly need some help in order to find their way to a seventh seed in the AFC.
The Texans would likely need the Steelers and the New England Patriots to lose three or four of their next seven games. Considering each of them has a backup-level quarterback set to start down the stretch, seeing such an outcome is far from impossible.
However, for the Texans to find the easiest route to the postseason, it relies on their ability to stack up as many wins as possible through their next seven games.
By the looks of it, a vast majority of those matchups appear to be winnable, but a loss in just one or two of those games makes the road quickly become a whole lot tougher.

title: Texans' Chances of Beating Ravens Look Strong Based on Week 12 Odds
full_text:
The Houston Texans put together their first home win in nearly 11 months during their Thursday Night Football matchup against the Indianapolis Colts .
And now as the Texans head into Week 12, it seems they're pretty strong favorites to come out with a second straight win against the Baltimore Ravens––at least based on initial betting odds.
The Texans enter the weekend as some of the heavier favorites to come out on top in their respective matchup, as Houston has started the week at -6.5 over the Ravens, per odds from FanDuel Sportsbook .
Despite the Texans' 4-6 record, it's actually the eighth game of the season that they stand out as the pregame favorites. Houston's 4-6 against the spread, and has hit the spread in four of their last six games.
The Ravens, however, have not been as kind against the spread.As Baltimore has fallen into a six-game losing streak, they've also failed to cover in five of their last six games.
They did narrowly cover at +2.5 in this past weekend's 33-35 loss to the Carolina Panthers, and in this one against Houston, they'll have a chance to do so once again as underdogs of just under a touchdown.
Odds refresh periodically and are subject to change.
If you or someone you know has a gambling problem and wants help, call 1-800-GAMBLER.
Just by the looks of this game on paper, the Texans are rolling into this game with all of the momentum on their side.
Houston's coming off a resounding Thursday night win over a division rival that's given them the benefit of a mini-bye , and a few days of extra rest over the Ravens.
The Texans will be at home, should be a bit healthier than they were this time last week, and have been performing better than Baltimore on both sides of the ball over the last few games.
As for the Ravens, they're on a six-game losing streak, have a combined point differential of -79 on that losing streak, and are still without their starting quarterback, Lamar Jackson. All momentum is leaning in the Texans' favor.
But, we have seen the Texans struggle in similar positions this season where it feels like all is going their way, just for them to fall flat on Sunday. Just look back to Week 7 against the New York Giants , or just a couple of weeks ago against the Cleveland Browns .
If the Texans can continue to produce as well as they have through the air behind MVP-level production from C.J. Stroud, the pass-rush can continue to produce, and the secondary keeps on trending upwards as it has been since the bye, it'll be tough for the Ravens to come out of Houston with a win.
It remains to be seen if the Texans will keep firing on all cylinders for a second straight week. But if they do, it'd certainly be another step in the right direction for their hopes of making a late run to a spot in the postseason.

title: What Woody Marks' Return Means for Texans Run Game vs. Ravens
full_text:
The Houston Texans' run game is set to get a bit of a facelift in their upcoming matchup against the Baltimore Ravens.
According to an update from Texans head coach DeMeco Ryans, the team is "hopeful" that Marks will return to the lineup in Week 12 after missing Thursday night's game against the Indianapolis Colts.
Marks has been in concussion protocol since the Texans' Week 10 game against the Cleveland Browns, in which he left and didn't return in the middle of the third quarter. Once Sunday against the Ravens arrives, Marks will be two weeks removed from that injury and should be good to go for his return to the field.
But for the Texans' run game, it'll be the first time that both Marks and Montgomery will be working in tandem with one another for the first time since Week 5 against the Tennessee Titans.
What can we expect from Houston on the ground as they'll be back to 100%? And will the backfield split be any different than what we last saw from when each of Marks and Montgomery were healthy at the start of the season?
Now, since the first four weeks of the season when the Texans had a collective 0-4 record, their run game has looked a lot better in the moments that Woody Marks or David Montgomery has led the operation by themselves.
However, we can look back to those first four weeks at the Texans were fully healthy in the backfield to get a better picture of what to expect for their running back split when both of their top guys are healthy.
From Weeks 1 through 4, Montgomery was on the field for an average of 54% of the Texans' offensive snaps and saw 47 total carries. Marks was out there for around 45% of the snaps and came away with 28 total carries.
So Montgomery, when both guys are healthy, is typically leading the way over Marks by a slight margin in snaps, but also takes a bulk of the Texans' carries in the backfield, while Marks operates as a pass-blocker and a more potent weapon in the receiving game.
However, based on how Montgomery operated in the Texans' last game against the Colts, maybe there's a route to him seeing a bit more than that 55% snap share.
There's a case that Montgomery should get a bigger workload in the Texans' offense moving forward because of how solid he looked against the Colts . And that outcome certainly remains a possibility if Montgomery continues to carry his efficiency into the next game against the Ravens.
However, at least initially, the Texans feel more likely to roll with their previous setup in the backfield at a 55-45 split and roll with the hot hand on a weekly basis, rather than simply lean on Montgomery more right off the bat.
Marks has been a solid weapon in the Texans' offense when he's been given the opportunities. He's a quick, home run hitter on the ground, can work well as a pass-catcher, and is an underrated pass-blocker that is deserving of seeing the ball in his hands to make plays on a weekly basis.
Houston has entrusted him with over 15 touches a game in every week that Montgomery has been sidelined, and it's hard to imagine he's totally taken out of the game plan moving forward now that the position looks a little bit healthier.
The one back in the Texans' offense who feels most likely to be taken out of the game plan is their now-third-string runner, Emari Demercado , who has taken around 25% of the offensive snaps to Marks and Montgomery when the other has been sidelined, but now feels due to see that number reach closer to zero.
Demercado has been a serviceable backup when the Texans have had him on the field this season, but he was only meant to be a plug-and-play veteran who stepped up due to injury.
Now that Houston is healthy in the backfield, Demercado reverts back to their RB3, and only sees looks on the offense if either of Marks or Montgomery is forced out for more time. There's a chance he could find some snaps on special teams so he's not a complete non-factor on the Texans' roster, though.

title: Texans Fantasy Football Check: Buy, Sell or Hold These 7 Players
full_text:
The Houston Texans have about seven weeks to go before their fate is decided on whether or not they'll be able to climb out of their current hole for an eventual playoff appearance.
But for fantasy football managers, the playoffs are right around the corner. Trade deadlines are approaching, and now marks a pivotal point in the year where roster decisions and big moves can have major implications for how championships shake out over the next several weeks.
So in the spirit of those fantasy football leagues heating up, now is as good a time as ever to take a step back to look at the Texans' roster and evaluate which players you might want to add to your fantasy team, who you might want to sell, and others that might be best to hold onto if you have them.
Let's break down the buy, sell, or hold case for seven players on the Texans roster and see who you really want to invest in for the home stretch of the season.
C.J. Stroud is the quarterback you want to have in fantasy football right now. Not only has he exploded onto the scene as QB5 through the first 11 weeks of the season, but he's also been extremely consistent over the last several games as well.
The Texans' signal-caller has scored 20 points or more in six of his last seven games. Stroud's been accurate, making good decisions, and scoring touchdowns— which is most important for his fantasy production.
Hang onto Stroud if you've got him, and if you need a quarterback, go out and find the guy who's got him.
Montgomery's coming off one of his best games of the season against the Indianapolis Colts, where the Texans running back found his way to a season-high 26 carries for 107 rushing yards, but didn't find the end zone.
On one hand, the game was extremely encouraging to see from Montgomery after he's been both injured and ineffective through the first half of the year. But Montgomery only has three 100-yard games to his name since 2024. The production he showcased on Thursday night probably isn't sustainable for the rest of the season, especially once Woody Marks returns from his concussion.
If there's an opportunity to sell high on Montgomery, now would be the perfect time to do so. At best, he's a high-end flex option to rely on for the rest of the season. There might not be many more times this season that the Texans back claims over 15 PPR fantasy points in a single week.
Woody Marks was out of the Texans' lineup this past week due to a concussion, but he's trending for a return in Week 12 against the Baltimore Ravens as he'll have had two weeks to fully get out of concussion protocol.
But will Marks be able to be utilized as a reliable fantasy option? It's hard to say. Marks wasn't the most effective running back to plug into lineups over the past several weeks that Montgomery was out with a groin injury––and now, he's back in the mix. Marks' carries will only slim from the point they've been at.
He's probably not worth much in a trade right now, and he's got too much appeal even as a running back in a committee to be truly droppable. So keep him as a bench stash, hoping that his upside as a pass-catcher can allow him to be usable in the future.
Nico Collins has had better years of production over the last three seasons, but the Texans' No. 1 wideout has finally begun to catch his stride over the last two weeks.
Collins has scored 14 or more PPR fantasy points over the last three weeks, and has found his way to a touchdown in each of those. In Week 10 against the Cleveland Browns, Collins found his way to a staggering 16 targets , turning those into 24.4 points.
With his big-play ability and nose for the end zone, Collins is someone who could continue to rise over the second half of the season and settle in as a quality WR2, even with the talent around him in the Texans’ wide receiver room.
Tank Dell certainly got many excited for what the second half of the season could hold for him once he saw over 100 yards in a game for the first time since his injury back in Week 9 against the LA Chargers. But since that performance, Dell has remained pretty quiet.
He's seen a combined six receptions for 48 yards over the last two games he's played, and has scored less than 10 PPR fantasy points in each of those. He's not exactly the more reliable play to plug in at receiver in your lineup, but not exactly someone to give up on just yet.
The Texans love utilizing Dell as a potent weapon in their passing game when the opportunities are there, and those looks will only increase as he gets more and more time on the field. Right now, he's best valued as a WR4/5, but with a couple of good games, he could rise back to a WR3/high-upside flex play.
Last week against the Colts was the quietest we've seen from Hutchinson in a while. He saw just two receptions for the second game this season, which resulted in his second-lowest point total of the year.
But Hutchinson could still be a low-end flex play to rely on for the next few weeks. Hutchinson has still brought in a touchdown in three of his last four games, and he stays on the field a considerable amount–– logging over 75% of the offensive snaps across the last three games of the season.
If he's out on waivers, he's a worthwhile pickup to stash on your bench, and could be forced into your lineup in a pinch, considering he's a frequently utilized option in a high-volume passing offense.
Schultz has been a bit of a non-factor in the Texans' receiving game over the last three games. He hasn't seen more than two receptions since before Houston's bye in Week 8, and has caught one touchdown on the season.
While the Texans tight end started off his season with an encouraging Week 2 contest against the Cincinnati Bengals with 26 PPR fantasy points, he's probably best served to be on waivers at this point in the year, only to be picked up if you're in desperate need of a spot-start at the position.

title: Texans Have Good Reason to Repeat Key O-Line Change in Week 12
full_text:
The Houston Texans went into their Week 11 game against the Indianapolis Colts preparing to roll out a different look than usual on their offensive line.
The plan was: rather than roll out one primary tackle on the right side of their line, the Texans would instead rotate their right tackle duties between two players throughout the night–– that being Trent Brown and Braden Smith.
Things didn't exactly go according to plan, though. In less than 10 snaps for Brown, he would leave the game with a back injury that was unable to return from. That led to Braden Smith holding things down on the right side of the line for most of the night against the Colts.
And overall, Smith had a rather impressive performance. In the 59 total snaps he saw, he allowed just two pressures, zero sacks, caused zero penalties, and led to David Montgomery rushing for a season-high 107 yards.
It was about as good of a performance the Texans have seen at their right tackle position all season long. It was also Smith's first time really holding the fort down as Houston's primary starter on the right side of the line. His opportunity finally came, and he delivered.
So now, it begs the question: will the Texans simply continue with Smith as their starting right tackle moving forward, will they hand the keys back to Brown, or will they re-try their plan of rotating both if each is healthy?
Throughout the first half of the season, the Texans' starter on the right side, Trent Brown, has remained serviceable in his role. Pro Football Focus grades him as the 32nd best run-blocking tackle (66.6) among 72 eligible players, but 50th overall (63.2).
But there are some glaring flaws within Brown's fit: he's highly penalized, he's allowed 24 pressures on the season, and his ability to be consistently available is questionable, to say the least.
Smith, however, has finally returned from his prior injury issues, stepped as the Texans' starter, and was exactly what the team has been looking for ever since they signed him to a $20 million deal this offseason: a positive run blocker, an improvement in pass protection, and someone who helps limit Houston's excessive penalties .
Smith was signed this offseason with the idea that he would step up as the Texans' starting right tackle, and now, he's finally showcased a bit of the vision Houston had when they brought him in less than a year ago.
Now, it's on Houston to continue giving him opportunities to start and be a positive force in what's been an up-and-down offensive line unit over the last few seasons.
Texans head coach DeMeco Ryans spoke about Smith's performance in Thursday's game against the Colts, crediting his ability to be a physical force in the run game.
"In the game on Thursday, I thought Braden did a good job, going out, playing physically," Ryans said. "It seemed he was excited to play. I just liked the play style, and how he was finishing downfield in the running game. That was also a contributing factor to us running the ball as well as we did."
Perhaps it may depend on what the health of both Smith and Brown looks like heading into the week against the Baltimore Ravens before the Texans make an official decision on who starts.
But based on Thursday's performance, it might be increasingly hard to keep Smith out of the lineup if he can continue to play as well as he did.
