title: Jaguars Made One Key Change vs. Giants That Shouldn't Go Unnoticed
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars have been flexible week in and week out under head coach Liam Coen over the last two seasons, and the trend continued in Week 11 against the New York Giants.
Dating back to even the early days of the Coen era, the Jaguars have been willing to adjust roles and strategies as the season goes on. They did it last season with Dyami Brown and Cole Van Lanen, and they have continued to do so this year as they fight their way to a potential top seed in the AFC. Not all changes are massive, but each is worth noting.
In the tough Week 11 loss to the New York Giants, the Jaguars made yet another change that should not go unnoticed: a change at punt returner.
While most of the conversation around Parker Washington's performance against the Giants has centered around the touchdown that wasn't, perhaps the most interesting note about his Week 11 is the fact that, for the first time in two years, he didn't play a single special teams snap. After serving as the Jaguars' top punt returner for the entirety of the Coen era, Washington didn't field a punt against the Giants, with veteran running back Ameer Abdullah instead taking his spot.
The Jaguars have toyed with using other returners at different points, such as with Travis Hunter returning punts in Week 8 against the Indianapolis Colts. But Washington still returned punts in that game, unlike in Week 11 against the Giants. After the Jaguars entering the season willing to use Washington on punt team each week, it appears their tune has changed as we get into the meat of the season.
“Yeah, I think that obviously, as Parker [Washington] continues to ascend and doing really good things for us, just trying to limit some of the hits that he may take and some of the different game plan and meetings and things that he has to be involved in and have a lot of trust in Ameer," Coen said Monday.
"He's done it throughout the course of his career, did a great job last night of fielding them and giving us a chance. We didn't cover great. We didn't block it great. Didn't give him too many opportunities. I thought their punter did a phenomenal job flipping the field on a number of different occasions. I definitely see Ameer being able to do it for us moving forward.”
This is notable for a few reasons. One big reason is that Washington entered the season as one of the best returners in the NFL. He returned two different punts for touchdowns last season and had a punt return for a touchdown in 2024 too. Washington's punt return numbers have been, well, brutal in 2026 (10 returns for 49 yards, long of 12), but he is an elite talent there.
But the Jaguars clearly know Washington is one of their most important pieces on offense. Outside of Trevor Lawrence, Washington has a case to be made as the offense's second-most vital piece. This move seems to reflect that the Jaguars agree.

title: Jaguars Stock Report: Giants Loss Raises New Concerns About Bhayshul Tuten's Injury
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars will need to get back on track in Week 12, and it will take a few different players flipping their trajectory to make it happen.
That is the case after most losses, but especially so for the Jaguars after their Week 11 loss to the New York Giants that saw them play sloppy football for most of the game. If the Jaguars are going to fix it next week, it is clear who will have to step back up.
With that in mind, here is our Jaguars stock report after Sunday's loss to the Giants, indicating who is trending upward, and who needs to bounce back.
Jaguars fans, I get it. You want sacks. I hear you. But, well, there is no real point in continuing to talk about the Jaguars' defensive scheme and what it asks of the Jaguars' defensive ends. The fact the Jaguars have one of the five best defenses in football and a 20-7 record dating back to the start of last season has changed zero minds about the Jaguars' success with the current scheme and how the lack of sacks, frankly, do not really matter at all.
Okay. Maybe I do not get it. With that said, the Jaguars' ends played great football on Sunday. Travon Walker had seven pressures and forced several off-target passes from J.J. McCarthy and drew some penalties as well. Hines-Allen had a sack, a forced fumble, and several other key plays as well. This was a strong effort from the Jaguars' star defensive ends, regardless of the hunger from the fans for sacks.
Some people may see Jordan Davis' 50% snap rate and wonder why he didn't play more, but he actually played quite a bit for the role he has in the Jaguars' defense. Considering the Jaguars' defense was much better with him on the field than it was with him on it, and considering the Jaguars put together a terrific day against the run, it is hard to imagine the trade for Davis didn't have a big first-week impact. He isn't going to rack up sacks, but he is already doing his job to change the Jaguars' run defense for the better.
Parker Washington might have had a touchdown robbed by the officials, but he still had a stellar outing. He put together his second-ever back-to-back 100-yard game, and he was a few tough contested catches against a good Giants secondary away from having another potential career day. When the Jaguars needed a big play, they went to Washington. Heck, they went to him when they didn't need a big play. Washington's status as the No. 1 wide receiver in Liam Coen's offense is as clear now as it has been all season long.
It is time for the Jaguars to sit Bhayshul Tuten until he is healthy. The Jaguars' star running back has shown a lot of toughness and grit by grinding through his foot/ankle injury over the last three games, but this game was proof that an injured Tuten does the Jaguars no favors when they are playing a team that can actually compete with them. It wasn't a problem against bad teams like the Baltimore Ravens and Tennessee Titans, but it was a problem Sunday.
The Jaguars are 1-5 in the Liam Coen era when Trevor Lawrence throws 40+ passes, and their lone win saw them score 17 points. The offense needs to be balanced to thrive, but the Jaguars can not find that balance without a healthy Tuten. He just did not look anything like himself against the Giants, and it is time for the Jaguars to take stock into what that could mean. The injury was a concern before. Now, it looks like it has to potential to change their entire trajectory as an offense.
Ezra Cleveland has been a good soldier for the Jaguars over the last few seasons, but he has not had the same success this year that he had a year ago. The Jaguars have still been able to put up a ton of points in the meantime, but we saw on Sunday (and in Week 2 against the Broncos) what happens when the Jaguars have to face blue-chip defensive linemen, and Cleveland is a big reason for the issues.
Cleveland had his worst game of the season, and one of his worst games with the Jaguars, on Sunday. He let up some pressures in the passing game and was far below what the Jaguars needed him to be as a run-blocker. Cleveland is looking more and more like a player who is reaching his final months with the franchise, because they will need to upgrade the right guard spot moving ahead.

title: The Good, Bad, and Ugly From Jaguars' Week 11: Trevor Lawrence's Day and Officiating Follies
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- Like with any NFL game, Week 11 provided the Jacksonville Jaguars with some good, some bad, and certainly some ugly.
The Jaguars dropped to 7-3 and saw their chances at the No. 1 seed take a serious hit due to a 23-18 loss to the New York Giants on Sunday. The loss revealed a few of the Jaguars' key issues, such as the state of the offensive line and running game, while also revealing some areas where the Jaguars have taken a step.
So, what was the good, the bad, and the ugly from the Jaguars' Week 11 loss on the road? We break it down below.
If there was one thing the Jaguars did exceptionally well on Sunday, it was stopping the run. Considering this was the debut of new nose tackle Jordan Davis, that is likely exactly what the Jaguars needed to see. The only success the Giants had running the ball Sunday came via J.J. McCarthy scrambles, and he really just had the one 22-yard scamper. Otherwise, he had six rushes for 11 yards. Eliminate McCarthy's lone long scramble, and the Giants rushed 24 times for 55 yards, an average of 2.29 yards per carry.
The deeper metrics speak to the success the Jaguars had, holding Giants running back Cam Skattebo to 14 carries for 34 yards. The Jaguars were the 2nd-best rush defense of Week 11 in terms of EPA/Play and 4th-best in terms of success rate. Perhaps the most encouraging sign, though, was that the Jaguars showed real improcement in the running game after back-to-back middling performances.
The Jaguars had their worst performance against the run in terms of EPA/Play of the year in Week 10 against the Tennessee Titans, while Week 9 against the Baltimore Ravens was their fifth-worst. The Giants were not far off from the Titans and Ravens in terms of rushing production and efficency entering Week 11, too, which means the Jaguars did not just suddenly get an easier opponent.
As you will see in the table below, the Jaguars had their best game against the run by far during their post-Davon Hamilton stretch. Losing Hamilton for the season was a massive blow, but the results from Week 11 indicate that the Jaguars have gotten back on track in terms of their run defense, and Davis likely played a big role in that.
Yards Before Contact/Attempt
Yards After Contact/Attempt
Considering the Jaguars are set to play the Titans and Tony Pollard again in Week 12, we should see just how far the Jaguars' run defense has come since their poor Week 10 showing. Then in Week 13, the Jaguars will be tested by Ben Johnson and the Chicago Bears. We will find out very soon whether the run defense is back to being elite, but it looked like it on Sunday.
The word I have used to describe Trevor Lawrence's performance against the Giants would be ... reckless. It is clear that this isn't a chicken or the egg situation; the Jaguars' offensive line was absolutely picked to pieces by Abdul Carter and the rest of the Giants' front from the first drive of the game, and Lawrence began to press as a result. It is likely not much of a coincidence that the Jaguars' two worst games on offense this season are the two games in which Lawrence has been pressured the most.
Looking at Lawrence's passing chart displays just how frustrating of a day it was for the Jaguars' franchise passer. Some quarterbacks get pressure and refuse to let go of the ball. Some get pressured and turn into Checkdown Charlie. But Lawrence is built differently than those quarterbacks, and his instinct is normally to keep chucking the ball downfield and, in this case, get even more aggressive.
Trevor Lawrence: Wk 11 Pass Chart pic.twitter.com/JQWhLDus4H
That aggressiveness came back to bite the Jaguars more than once. Lawrence's two interceptions were arguably his two worst throws of thes eason, and he had several other passes that looked like they could have been intercepted as well. It is clear why Lawrence struggled, but it is also clear that the Jaguars' offense is not built to win without Lawrence playing at a high level. When he struggles, the entire unit struggles, and that is what we saw on Sunday.
This is the last time we are going to harp on the officials. Really!
The Jaguars had plenty of their own ugly on Sunday. The offensive line and overall protection plan was terrorized off the jump, and Carter looked like prime Von Miller for four quarters as a result. But it is hard not to think the officials were the worst part of this game, and it isn't even just because of the Parker Washington touchdown that never was. A few things from Sunday that didn't include Washington's call:
“Yeah, challenging for sure to lose one of your challenges, for that. Everybody makes mistakes, just as we do; mistakes are made," Coen said on Monday.
"Everybody makes mistakes," is for when your teenager puts a dent in the car. It is for when you sneeze on the salad bar. It is not for the National Football League. This was a maddening game to watch from purely an operational standpoint, and the NFL has a big problem considering this may not have even been the worst-officiated game of the Jaguars' season.

title: Jaguars Have Another Reason to Be Frustrated With NFL After Parker Washington TD Controversy
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars are ready to move on from Week 11. That doesn't mean everybody else is, though.
The lasting conversation from the Jaguars' 23-18 loss to the New York Giants in Week 11 rests firmly on the Parker Washington touchdown that wasn't. It has been talked about to death to this point, but for good reason.
With a bit over 12 minutes left in a 20-6 game, Washington appeared to catch a touchdown pass to make it a one-score game, but it was ruled incomplete on the field and then again upon review after the Jaguars challenged it. From the broadcast to even players in the Giants locker room, it felt like a clear catch that, for some reason, wasn't called.
Giants safety Jevon Holland on this play: "The game's over — that might have been a catch. That was a hell of a play. I thought he got his foot down, I was like, 'Damn.' But then they called it out and I was like, 'Shit, all right.' Shout-out Vegas. I don't know." https://t.co/Eid1ANMGOp
While the Jaguars are ready to move onto Week 12 and the Tennessee Titans, though, Monday Night Football provided yet another reason for the Jaguars and their base to be frustrated with the NFL's lack of consistency and accountability.
While the Washington non-touchdown looked silly in the moment, and even sillier later in the night when Mike Evans was given a touchdown catch on a play that looked a lot less secure than Washington's, Monday Night Football took it to a different level.
During the Bengals' loss to the Washington Commanders, Joe Burrow threw a touchdown to Tee Higgins that looked almost exactly like the Washington play in terms of ball movement and how Higgins got his feet in-bounds. The difference, of course, is that Higgins and the Bengals were awarded a touchdown ... while the Jaguars had to settle for a field goal due to a missed call.
It, again, came to the point where both the broadcast team and their official rules analyst agreed that Washington should have been awarded a touchdown ... which happened during the Jaguars game as well. In short, the Jaguars seemingly got jobbed, while the Bengals (and 49ers the night before) didn't.
Joe Buck: "Parker Washington and the Jacksonville Jaguars are thinking, well, why is that a touchdown, and why was Parker's ruled incomplete in that loss yesterday to the Giants, Russell Yurk?" Russell Yurk: "I like both that play and this play as catches..." https://t.co/iXrBDLvihn pic.twitter.com/OGt2LF9KQe
To the Jaguars' credit, none of the members of the locker room or coaching staff have outright complained about the call or pointed to it as the reason they lost. They are correct in doing so, because that call is far from the singular reason why the Jaguars lost that game.
“I mean, because we know that one play didn't make or break the situation, right? It was an accumulation of mistakes that we feel like we made, plus them actually coming out to play and being on their stuff," Jaguars wide receiver Jakobi Meyers said on Monday.
"The game is deeper than one play. Yeah, the game is just deeper than one play, so we know that wasn't going to be the one that defined it. We just got to make the ones that do matter and hope that they do come our way in the future.”
But for as much truth as there is in that, there is even more truth in understanding that the NFL made the wrong call, and everything they have done since has only made that clearer.

title: Jaguars Week 11 Snap Count Analysis: Bhayshul Tuten's Injury Demands Solutions
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars have some questions to answer after arguably their worst loss of the season.
The Jaguars fell to the New York Giants 23-18 in one of the sloppiest games the Jaguars have played in the Liam Coen era, racking up penalties and self-inflicted mistakes at an unsustainable rate. The Jaguars still sit at 7-3, but this game clearly could have, and should have, played out differently.
"Clearly, not prepared well enough as we have been, maybe had too many things in, moving parts," Coen said after the game. "That's a direct reflection of me, and making sure that these guys are prepared well enough. We had been prepared in the majority of our football games, I felt like, and that did not show tonight, especially early on. I put that directly on me."
What could the Jaguars have done differently in the tough road loss? We take a look at some of the Jaguars' snap counts to try to find some of those answers.
It is clear the Jaguars are not getting the same version of Bhayshul Tuten that they were earlier in the season, and it is completely injury related. Tuten was one of the best and most productive running backs in football through the first eight weeks of the 2026 season, but a foot/ankle injury over the last three weeks have hurt his numbers and, as a result, hurt the rest of the offense that in many ways flows through the running game.
Tuten played his second-lowest snap count of the season with 31 snaps (43%), which saw Chris Rodriguez Jr. play 27 snaps (38%). But even with the snaps closer to a true 50/50 split this week than most others, Tuten still got a good bit more touches than Rodriguez, who finished the game with just four carries. Tuten left the game twice after getting stepped on, and it certainly seems like the Jaguars could reevaluate things.
“Yeah, we'll see. The recheck today wasn't too bad. Obviously got stepped on in the game a few times, I think twice on the same play, so that re-aggravated it for sure. So, we're definitely having some of those conversations," Coen said Monday.
"He's tough as nails. He wants to play. He wants to continue to fight and give us the best chance to be able to go. We'll have some more of those conversations and see what he looks like when he gets out there running around or moving around on Wednesday and Thursday. Let it play out throughout the week and knowing that he probably won't be able to do a ton for us like he hasn't been for the last few weeks in practice. So really it'll be a business as usual throughout the week for Tuten, and then we'll just kind of see where we're at towards the end of the week.”
The Jaguars have long leaned on Parker Washington as their punt returner, but there was a bit of a shift in that department on Sunday. Jaguars running back Ameer Abdullah played 10 special teams snaps on Sunday, but four of those snaps were as a punt returner. Abdullah had not returned a single punt for the Jaguars all season long until Sunday when he ended up returning four punts for 23 yards (5.8 yards per attempt), a change-up from Washington as punt returner.
Washington played zero special teams snaps for the first time since Week 17 in the 2024 season, meaning Sunday was the first time during the entire Liam Coen era that he was not a big piece of Heath Farwell's unit. This sure looks like a change that could stick, considering what Coen said when asked about Abdullah at the returner spot on Monday.
“Yeah, I think that obviously, as Parker [Washington] continues to ascend and doing really good things for us, just trying to limit some of the hits that he may take and some of the different game plan and meetings and things that he has to be involved in and have a lot of trust in Ameer," Coen said. "He's done it throughout the course of his career, did a great job last night of fielding them and giving us a chance. We didn't cover great. We didn't block it great. Didn't give him too many opportunities. I thought their punter did a phenomenal job flipping the field on a number of different occasions. I definitely see Ameer being able to do it for us moving forward.”
The Jaguars saw Jordan Davis (35 snaps, 50%) and Jessie Bates III (66 snaps, 94%) make their official Jaguars debuts, and the difference made by Davis at least was clear. The Giants averaged under 2.0 yards per carry when Davis was on the field and did not have a rush longer than five yards, giving him a clear impact made through his first day. Meanwhile, Bates played every snap but the few snaps when the Jaguars were in a goal line defense and had their heavy personnel on the field.
Davis played 52% of the snaps for the Eagles this year before the trade and his career-high was the 61% of snaps he played during the 2025 season, so him playing 50% of the snaps snaps in his debut made plenty of sense. Jaguars starting nose tackle Davon Hamilton played over 50% of the snaps just twice in six full games his season, and he hit the number just seven times in 17 games in 2025.
“Yeah, I thought both guys did their jobs well. I thought specifically Jordan and [DT] Davon Godchaux did some really good things up front in terms of allowing our second level guys to play freely. Our linebackers were free a lot in the run game. They disrupted some things," Coen said.
"I think Jessie just didn't have a ton of ops. Like there wasn't a lot of balls his way. He got kind of moved on the double move there that they ended up not hitting. But, nothing really stood out in terms of glaring negatives and nothing really stood out as like obviously big-time playmaking or anything that way. But fully anticipate those guys to be able to continue to help us, and they're going to make some plays for our team. I don’t doubt that whatsoever”

title: Chiefs vs. Bills: NFL Week 12 Preview, Score Predictions for Thanksgiving
full_text:
After a somewhat light start to the season on the schedule front, it's about to get real for the Kansas City Chiefs. Awaiting them on Thanksgiving Day is one of their perceived top threats in the conference, the Buffalo Bills.
In a classic tilt between all-world quarterbacks, dynamic head coaches and elite rushing attacks, many are calling for bushels of points on Thursday. On the other hand, an ugly weather report for the holiday may have different plans.
With kickoff on the horizon, which side will come out on top? The Kansas City Chiefs On SI crew makes its predictions for Week 12 of the regular season.
Joshua Brisco: This has been true for a large number of Chiefs-Bills matchups in the past, but this game truly feels like a coin-flip. The loss of Kenneth Walker matters, but the Bills have unanswered questions on both sides of the ball. Buffalo wins these regular-season showdowns, but it’s arguably more important for Kansas City this time through.
The Chiefs’ offensive tackles are cause for concern, but Patrick Mahomes has been playing tremendous football behind that same line for much of this season. James Cook is a weapon, but Steve Spagnuolo’s defense is typically stout against the run. Ultimately, this feels like a game that comes down to a late field goal or a fourth-quarter turnover.
I’m relatively confident that this game will live up to the hype, but I could easily see either team escaping with the narrow victory.
Jordan Foote: In my Week 12 preview, I echoed Brisco's sentiment and chalked this one up to a relative coin-flip as well. The Bills have plenty of holes on their roster and, in many ways, remind me of this Chiefs squad. Usually, having home-field advantage would be the deciding factor in a game like this, but Buffalo simply doesn't look like a club that's firing on all cylinders.
The Kansas City defense will surely be put to the test against the dynamic rushing duo of Allen and Cook. There also may not be a more lethal play extender than Allen in the dropback game when he's operating at peak capacity. Still, the Chiefs have a running game of their own with Johnson enjoying some success. A heavy ball-control style of outing goes to KC.
Expect a close one at the new Highmark Stadium. I'm not rolling with a combined 60-plus points, instead giving the visitors a one-score edge thanks to either a timely stop on defense or some Mahomes magic on the other side of the football.
Joshua Schulman: The Chiefs are looking to change their fortunes against the Bills in the regular season. Patrick Mahomes may own Josh Allen in the postseason, but he’s 1-5 against Buffalo in regular-season meetings.
With Kenneth Walker out for the third consecutive week, Emmett Johnson will take on a larger workload in his place. He’ll need to have a big day with cold temperatures and heavy rainfall expected in Buffalo.
While the Chiefs have bounced back in a huge way since their two-game losing skid, they haven’t faced much competition. Behind Buffalo’s defense improved defense and a rowdy home crowd, I think it’ll be tough for the Chiefs to pull this one off.
Tyler Brown: This is the kind of game that comes down to the last possession, and I think it ends up going Kansas City’s way despite Mahomes’ 1-5 record against Allen in the regular season. I think they match up that well. Allen is playing somewhat erratically, as shown by his nine touchdowns and nine interceptions over the past eight games.
The Bills’ defense has looked great against backup quarterbacks, but it allows more than 30 points a game against good-to-average offenses, and Kansas City is as good as any. Mahomes has been dealing for a month, and he should find openings against a vulnerable defensive backfield. With Emmett Johnson carrying the load, the rushing attack will keep the Bills guessing. Travis Kelce, Josh Downs, and Rashee Rice can do the rest.
It will not be easy to stop Allen, and you have to account for Cook as well. Allen always seems to find another gear against this team, and the Chiefs will have to keep him out of the red zone, where he is a touchdown vulture. But in a possible Thanksgiving shootout in the rain, I like the team that appears more balanced.
The Chiefs have only one win against a team with a winning record, so this could be fool’s gold, but the process behind their recent surge looks legitimate.

title: Five Things the Chiefs Should Be Thankful For This Thanksgiving
full_text:
While the Kansas City Chiefs are in their final hours of preparation before facing off with the Buffalo Bills on Thanksgiving night , the holiday is a good time to reflect on some things that have gone well through the first 10 games of the season.
What's worth being thankful for in Chiefs Kingdom? There are some obvious blessings and some more surprising developments that all deserve a seat at the table.
In one of the quieter revelations of the Chiefs' season, rookie No. 6 overall pick Mansoor Delane and second-year third-rounder Nohl Williams have quickly developed into one of the league's best cornerback duos . While Delane has been managing an ongoing shoulder ailment, Williams has taken the second-most defensive snaps on the team in 2026.
With the exception of an understandably tough day against Jaxon Smith-Njigba, Delane has looked like every bit of a No. 1 NFL cornerback, and I'd argue that Delane still looked completely qualified against the Seahawks. Smith-Njigba got the best of the rookie, but the Delane wasn't lost against the reigning Offensive Player of the Year. Meanwhile, Williams has been consistently excellent on the other side of the field.
Anything stand out? https://t.co/tkIqLr6oHs pic.twitter.com/eg4H7W39Mx
Arguably the most thrilling part about the rise of this duo? Williams is under contract through the 2028 season, maxing out at a $2 million cap hit, while Delane's four-year, $42 million deal runs through 2029, with a fifth-year option for 2030.
Not only do the Chiefs have an excellent pair of starters right now, they have a young tandem that should continue to grow in years to come.
It was obvious that the Chiefs had to add a wide receiver before the NFL trade deadline , and Josh Downs appeared to be one of the only realistic options. While that wasn't an ideal place to begin negotiating, Downs' immediate impact has been impressive .
Not only has Downs been quick to pick up the playbook, he's brought an ease to the field in his first two games as a Chief.
With all of the necessary disclaimers about a small sample size and the quality of the Chiefs' opponents the last two weeks, I've been struck by how comfortable Downs looks in the Chiefs' offense, and even more excited by how quickly Patrick Mahomes decided to start going Downs' way.
Mahomes targeted Downs 10 times in two games for eight catches, 112 yards and a touchdown, and it never looked difficult or out-of-sync. Even as someone who was optimistic about what Downs could bring as a man-coverage-beater and a quarterback-friendly target, I thought it could be weeks before we saw the trickle-down effect of his addition to the receiver room. It took only a few reps before it became clear.
Now, the Chiefs can retool their receiving rotation , and the other pass-catchers should see less attention from opposing teams when Downs establishes himself as the biggest threat on a given play. There's still much more to prove in the weeks to come, but it would be hard to ask for anything more from Downs after such a short time in Kansas City.
Defensive end George Karlaftis has been a steadily improving player throughout his time in the NFL, but last season, while dealing with a thumb/hand injury ( a broken hand, according to D-line coach Joe Cullen ), Karlaftis appeared to plateau. With the injury behind him, Karlaftis has taken another step forward in 2026.
Karlaftis leads the team with eight sacks, 12 tackles for loss and 26 quarterback hits through 10 games, and many advanced stats support the box score .
NFL Pass Rusher Efficiency Week 1-11 Greg Rousseau is a machine #BillsMafia #Skol #ChiefsKingdom pic.twitter.com/bjfGvvbRVW
Will Karlaftis continue to evolve into one of the league's preeminent menaces off the edge? It's still too early to know that for sure. But if he can continue to be the player he's shown himself to be through the last few weeks, he'll be a foundational piece for years to come.
Most sacks since Week 8: 1. George Karlaftis - 7.0 2. Jeffery Simmons - 5.0* 2. Quinnen Williams - 5.0 *Joined Bears in Week 8 (had bye in Week 10)
Before Kenneth Walker suffered the groin injury that will hold him out for at least three games, including tonight's showdown in Buffalo, Walker would be the rightful holder of this No. 2 spot. Chiefs fans should still be enormously grateful for Walker's role on this team, of course—his early-season Offensive Player of the Year candidacy was completely legitimate, and the Chiefs will be better when Walker returns.
With that being said, rookie fifth-round pick Emmett Johnson has been extremely valuable to the Chiefs' offense, particularly in Walker's absence .
It's not just that Johnson has recorded back-to-back 100-yard rushing games in his two starts against the Atlanta Falcons and Arizona Cardinals. His 345 receiving yards are the third-most on the team, but that's not his best contribution either. The most valuable thing that Johnson has brought to the offense is normalcy, consistency and competence that allows the Chiefs to continue being an effective running team even without their superstar free agent addition.
When teams lose their only noteworthy running back (or when they enter a season without a back of that caliber), it becomes hard to respect the running game and easy to fall into an aggressively pass-happy offense, allowing defenses to assume one-dimensionality. Johnson has been better than just normal, consistent and competent, but that's what has allowed him to stay on the field, earning him more opportunities to make big plays while the threat of the run remains legitimate in Kansas City.
No need to overthink No. 1.
Mahomes has been phenominal so far this season, and he's playing at an MVP-caliber level after tearing his ACL and LCL in Week 15 of the 2025 season . It's easy to forget how uncertain Mahomes' future was after last year's season-ending injury because it was evident by the time training camp began that Mahomes would be starting in Week 1. Still, Mahomes' return shouldn't be taken for granted. Nor should his play.
There's been plenty of talk about the Chiefs' weaknesses at wide receiver before they made the trade to add Downs, but the most underrated part of Mahomes' season comes with how he's navigated a borderline-disastrous offensive tackle situation .
Pick your choice of offensive line pass protection grading metrics —often subjective, to be fair—and you'll find the Chiefs near the bottom of most of them. Meanwhile, Mahomes has been sacked only 13 times this year, tied for 28th-most in the league.
According to Warren Sharp , Mahomes has been sacked on just 10.4% of his pressures, the best rate in the league among Sharp's long list of qualifying quarterbacks.
Year after year, Mahomes maximizes his surroundings and overcomes the team's deficiencies so effectively that many people around the league forget that the Chiefs have any weaknesses at all. Mahomes improves Kansas City's ceiling and floor every season. Every Chiefs fan should be thankful for that.

title: Part 11: Chiefs-Bills Matchups Will Always Come Down to Mahomes and Allen
full_text:
The real football season officially starts now. After t hree straight games against middling opponents , the Kansas City Chiefs travel to face the Buffalo Bills in what both teams could bill as the biggest game of the season.
Both teams have played softer schedules up to this point, so we don't really know who they are. The Bills are 9-1, the Chiefs are 8-2, and the winner will hold the AFC's No. 1 seed at the end of the night. The forecast calls for 38 degrees and rain, and it doesn't get much more football on Thanksgiving than that.
The stakes are high, as usual, whenever these two teams and these two quarterbacks meet. Patrick Mahomes and Josh Allen are tied 5-5 in head-to-head matchups, and each meeting feels like an “ESPN Classic."
History says Buffalo has the upper hand. The Bills are at home in their brand-new stadium, and Allen is 5-1 against Mahomes in the regular season. That has worked out fine for the Chiefs, though, since they are 4-0 against Allen in the playoffs.
Both teams made offseason changes that were just shy of sweeping. Buffalo fired longtime head coach Sean McDermott and replaced him with his former offensive coordinator, Joe Brady. The Chiefs shook up their offensive coaching staff and added running backs Kenneth Walker and Emmett Johnson , which completely changed the dynamic of that unit.
Sometimes the biggest matchup in a game is the most obvious one, and when these two quarterbacks meet, the conversation starts and ends with them. Let’s dig in.
Mahomes is going scorched earth right now, but it goes without saying that the Chiefs need to stick with what has made them the No. 1 offense in the NFL: establishing and dominating with their rushing attack. The Bills are top 10 in rushing yards allowed per game, but they are much closer to the middle of the pack in yards per carry. In the end, Emmett Johnson will be critical, but Week 12 is all about one guy.
The Bills are fifth in total offense and second in points per game, averaging more than 31, and Mahomes will have to keep up. If Kansas City is going to outpace Buffalo, it will need its two-time MVP to play like one. The timing is good, too, with Mahomes averaging more than 300 yards per game and a 13-0 touchdown-to-interception ratio over his last four contests.
He should find success at all three levels. According to PFF, all of the Bills' starting linebackers allow more than 73 percent of their targets to be caught. Safety Cole Bishop, who always seems to have his best game against Kansas City, allows a 101.9 passer rating when targeted. Slot cornerback Dee Alford is allowing 13.4 yards per catch, which suits Travis Kelce, Josh Downs , and Rashee Rice well.
On the outside, Davison Igbinosun is playing good football for a rookie but has eight penalties, among the league's worst. Christian Benford is getting picked on the most, leading the team with 312 yards and four touchdowns allowed, and Maxwell Hairston has also struggled at times.
It depends on how much Andy Reid wants to get into his bag for a regular-season game, but he could have a fun time drawing up a game plan against this defense. It ranked among the league's worst in most categories before a recent stretch against the Ravens, Vikings, Jets, and Dolphins, all of which were played with backup quarterbacks, aside from Geno Smith.
If you lump those games in with their game against the Chargers, they are allowing just 10.6 points per game. In the other five games, against above-average to good offenses, they have allowed 31.6 points per game, and it is safe to say the Chiefs belong in that category, if not at the top.
If Mahomes wants to stake a claim to his third MVP season, he'll need a big performance on the biggest stage against another MVP quarterback. With running back Kenneth Walker out again, Mahomes can use his weaponry, which is gelling by the week, to light up the scoreboard and move his team to 9-2.
Allen is in another MVP race this season, and while he is not having his best year through the air, Steve Spagnuolo summed him up on Monday: "It just seems like, when he plays the Kansas City Chiefs, he's on fire. He becomes Superman."
This season, Allen has 14 touchdowns and nine interceptions and is averaging just over 252 yards per game, but as usual, you also have to watch his legs. He averages more than 29 rushing yards per game, though that number is inflated by his 121 yards against the Rams.
With Spagnuolo flipping on that film this week, it's fair to wonder whether we'll see more of second-year linebacker Jeffrey Bassa, who has at times come in to spy the quarterback. The other key is keeping the Bills outside of the three-yard line. Allen has 11 rushing touchdowns this year, and all but one have come from inside that area.
Through the air, this will be a big test for slot corner Chris Roland-Wallace. Allen's favorite targets are slot receiver Khalil Shakir and tight end Dalton Kincaid. On the outside, Nohl Williams, Mansoor Delane, and Kristian Fulton will have to shut down D.J. Moore, who has long been a reliable security blanket for many quarterbacks. Third-year wide receiver Keon Coleman is also on pace for a career season.
Allen and the offense operate best when running back James Cook gets into rhythm, so the Chiefs' front seven will be critical in forcing the Bills into passing situations. Nick Bolton, Drue Tranquill, and the defensive line are having career years in that area, which should help put Allen in compromising spots.
The multi-time All-Pro quarterback has thrown the sixth-most interceptions this season and ranks fifth in turnover-worthy plays with 18, according to PFF. The Chiefs match up fairly well in this game, but in a regular-season game, you never know what you will get from Reid's club, and you can bet your bottom dollar that Allen will put his best foot forward.

title: Chiefs Confidence Meter: How I Feel About the Team Against Bills in Week 12
full_text:
The football world knew it was going to be a critical matchup when it got announced, but finally arriving at the moment is an entirely different ballgame. Does it get any better than the Kansas City Chiefs and Buffalo Bills squaring off on Thanksgiving?
Week 12's nightcap for the Thursday portion sees head coach Andy Reid's crew take the field in Orchard Park against first-year head coach Joe Brady. In a battle of two MVP candidate quarterbacks who are backed by some of the more prolific rushing attacks in the sport, the only thing that can slow this one down is the weather.
Let's break down how both sides match up and put a bow on this Week 12 preview with a confidence meter rating on a scale ranging from 1-10.
After losing wide receiver Tyquan Thornton to a dislocated ankle earlier this season, the Kansas City aerial attack relied on short-range passes far too often. Quarterback Patrick Mahomes' average depth of target became a massive talking point as a result, but he's done some nice work to alleviate those concerns during the club's three-game winning streak.
The test now becomes doing it against a Buffalo defense that revamped its scheme over the course of the offseason and has looked better than expected. Even with a lackluster secondary, the Bills' defensive front is disruptive, led by edge rusher Greg Rousseau. Buffalo stacks the box at a 27.7% rate, good for seventh in the sport, and also runs stunts more often (36.7%) than any other NFL team.
Mahomes' sack avoidance is as good right now as it's ever been — he may need it on Thursday. With right tackle Jaylon Moore out and veteran Fred Johnson not being fully acclimated yet, it's unclear what the offensive line plan will be opposite the trio of rookie Kahlil Benson.
For the third straight week, the Chiefs are without star running back Kenneth Walker III . Normally, that'd put them well behind the proverbial eight-ball, but rookie Emmett Johnson's been fantastic in relief. In his first two professional starts, the Nebraska product has averaged 5.71 yards per touch while flashing his patented tough, elusive style out of the backfield.
Finding ways to stay ahead of the sticks and perhaps establish some deception could be the Chiefs' best friend. Given that it'll be a cold and nasty night at Highmark Stadium, keeping the ball on the ground makes ample sense. It'll only continue to be the case if Kansas City moves the ball against a defense that's 25th in early-down success rate at 45.7%.
Patience could be a virtue in the passing game as well. Per NFL Pro , Buffalo's operated split-safety shells on defense in 57.5% of dropbacks in the previous 10 meetings with the Chiefs, which is almost 10% higher than its mark against other clubs. Cover-1 has been the team's flavor of choice more recently.
Of course, the Chiefs are quite familiar with what Allen's capable of. The superstar signal-caller hasn't played up to his normal standard in the last few weeks, but all it takes is a brief look at his performances against Kansas City in the past to sweep that under the rug.
In the regular season, Allen owns a 99.4 passer rating with 11 touchdowns to three interceptions when facing the Chiefs. In the postseason, despite being 0-4, he's thrown for nine touchdowns and just a single interception. He's insanely dangerous, as defensive coordinator Steve Spagnuolo knows all too well:
On 4th & 2 with 2:27 left in regulation, Josh Allen dropped back before breaking off a 26-yard TD run. Allen had just a 1.2% chance of scoring a touchdown once he tucked the ball to run. It was Allen's first scramble TD run against the Chiefs in his career. Powered by @awscloud pic.twitter.com/xGduuXq6Bb
A key tendency clash in this one might be the blitz. Kansas City has allowed -0.150 EPA/dropback when bringing the heat, the third-best mark in the sport. Allen's output declines by 0.23 EPA/dropback when blitzed this season, so it's something to keep an eye on for Spagnuolo's group.
As far as the ground game is concerned, that's obviously where Buffalo butters its bread. The offensive line produces the most yards before contact per carry (2.2) on average for halfback James Cook, which pairs well with his explosive tendencies. Cook has rushed for at least 75 yards and a touchdown in nine straight outings, setting an NFL record.
Wrapping everything up here, the Bills love to get under center (second) and use the threat of the run in play action (first). That's helped them achieve the fourth-highest explosive run rate (12.4%), as well as a league-leading explosive pass clip (13.2%), even with an unassuming cast of wide receivers.
It'll be interesting to see how the Chiefs, who have struggled in the past with play-action and also go to their sub-packages frequently, aim to slow down the Buffalo attack. Working in the Chiefs' favor is a lethal cornerback duo of Nohl Williams and Mansoor Delane, in addition to a sound run defense up front.
Jeff Rodgers is in his first year as the Bills' special teams coordinator, possessing experience with the Arizona Cardinals and multiple other organizations in the past. According to Pro Football Focus , this is the No. 2-graded special teams unit in the sport. There's some evidence to back that up.
Only one team starts with better average field position on the offensive side of the ball than Buffalo at its own 33.4-yard line. Elsewhere, placekicker Tyler Bass is 24-of-25 on boots this year, including being perfect inside the 50, and the return duo of wideout Greg Dortch (20 punt bring-backs for 185 yards) and running back Ray Davis (league-leading 30.1 yards per kickoff return) must be accounted for.
Punter Tommy Doman is in eighth place among qualified players at his position with an average of 43.6 net yards per try. A healthy 40.9% of his attempts have landed inside the 20-yard line, with his 9.1% touchback rate trailing Chiefs punter Matt Araiza's 17.1% clip (NFL's highest) by quite a bit.
On the Chiefs' side, kicker Harrison Butker turned in a vintage performance in Week 11 by drilling all of his field goals and extra points. Perhaps he's beginning to turn a corner after a brutal start to the campaign that practically forced Kansas City to bring in competition .
As is usually the case in a Chiefs-Bills tilt, this one feels pretty much like the flip of a coin . Whenever Mahomes and Allen go toe-to-toe, just about anything can happen considering how elite they are at their best.
The difference, in this writer's view, is that we've seen the best of Mahomes more — and more recently — than that of Allen. Not even the loss of Walker can convince me that the Chiefs' offense will completely sputter in what figures to be a scoring environment that is far from ideal.
Ironically, and this may not be the case beyond Week 12, it's the Kansas City defense that might deserve more attention. Via Aaron Schatz , the average offensive DVOA faced by Spagnuolo's collective before Thanksgiving was dead last. Moving forward, including Thursday, it's the most difficult. If that doesn't scream "show me your true colors," I'm not sure what will.
Those in Chiefs circles will soon learn plenty about what this year's team is made of. The last three victories, no matter how impressive, didn't teach anyone something new. There are several paths to both of these AFC powerhouses coming away with wins on Thanksgiving, although siding with the visitors' lack of self-inflicted wounds gives them a slight edge.

title: Kenneth Walker Ruled Out for Thanksgiving Game: What It Means for the Chiefs
full_text:
For the third consecutive game, the Kansas City Chiefs will be rolling with a fifth-round rookie to lead the backfield. Star running back Kenneth Walker III was officially ruled out for Kansas City's Thanksgiving Day game vs. the Bills this morning due to a lingering groin injury . He has now missed three consecutive contests without a clear timetable for his recovery.
#Chiefs RB Kenneth Walker (groin) will be OUT for Thursday night’s game vs the Bills, per @Schultz_Report pic.twitter.com/rezzlryEp2
When Walker initially missed last week's game against the Cardinals, the expectation was that the team was holding him out to get some extra rest before Thanksgiving. However, it appears the turnaround was too quick to overcome. KC must lean on Johnson heavily once again.
In Walker's absence, Johnson has been nothing short of spectacular . The Nebraska product rushed for over 100 yards in both of his starts and found the end zone on three different occasions. Tomorrow's showdown will be a lot different, though, since the Bills have a much more formidable defense than Atlanta or Arizona. ESPN's Jeffri Chadiha revealed that Walker is dealing with a Grade 2 groin injury, which typically requires two to three weeks of rest. Since he first felt the symptoms two Fridays ago, it will have been nearly 21 days since the discomfort began.
It's uncertain whether the Chiefs are keeping Walker out as a precautionary measure or if he's still seriously injured. He was moving pretty gingerly in clips that surfaced online from yesterday's practice session, despite being listed as a limited participant. Additionally, he missed the team's walkthrough on Monday.
The :17 seconds of the open portion of practice where Kenneth Walker was doing something other than standing/stretching. #Chiefs pic.twitter.com/96VDcrxLhi
Offensive coordinator Eric Bieniemy made it known earlier this week that if Walker were to return, he would retain his job as the Chiefs' starting running back . Regardless, the coaching staff must wait at least one more game before getting the two tailbacks on the field together.
This development shouldn't massively impact the outcome of Thursday's matchup. The weather in Buffalo tomorrow is expected to be cold and rainy, which would create less-than-ideal conditions for a hampered Walker to return to action. The real concern is that a seemingly minor injury has turned into a near IR-length absence. The Chiefs have the utmost confidence in Johnson to hold down the fort while Walker recovers. Johnson has a chance to become a Thanksgiving Day legend if he can continue to produce at a high level.

title: Chargers Get Back Preseason Star: What Does This Mean for Donte Jackson and the DBs?
full_text:
The Los Angeles Chargers may be 1-9 and looking toward the offseason for a rebuild, but some positive news found its way to the mass media, giving Chargers fans a small boost of hope for the future.
Prior to the NFL season, the Chargers signed undrafted rookie cornerback Avery Smith out of Toledo . This was viewed as one of the best undrafted rookie signings across the league, with the hope that Smith would make the Bolts' roster.
As a prospect, Chargers draft expert Thomas Martinez described Smith as: "a well built defensive back but is on the shorter side at just over 5'10. He relies on instincts and route recognition to make plays on the ball and does an excellent job at preventing wide receivers from stacking him on deep routes. His tackling could use some technique improvement but he is unafraid and willing to get in the mix."
During the offseason and preseason, Smith was constantly being brought up as one of the flashy players who was making a real case to make the final 53-man roster. During the preseason, Smith recorded 15 tackles and a pass deflection, showing good downhill tackling ability and the competitive nature needed for playing defensive back, especially as an undersized player at the position.
With Smith trending to make the roster, the Chargers instead decided to hear out a phone call from the Seattle Seahawks, another team that had interest in the now proven-preseason standout for trade offers.
A trade went through , with the Seattle Seahawks giving the Chargers a 2027 sixth-round pick in exchange for Smith.
While Chargers fans were sad to see the standout star go, they were happy to see the team essentially get a sixth-round pick for free, since they did not draft or spend major cap space on the Toledo product.
A couple of short months later, the Chargers seem to have won the trade even more after recent events transpired.
Smith played six games with the Seahawks, recording five tackles and 56 special teams snaps. On Nov. 24, the team released Smith to make way for offensive tackle Chase Lundt . In one of the best moves the Chargers have made all season, the team saw their struggling and injured defensive back room and a former preseason standout who knows the system, and decided to sign Smith back to their roster.
Chargers claimed CB Avery Smith off waivers Wednesday, per the transaction wire. They had traded Smith to Seattle on cutdown day in August for a 2027 6th round draft pick. Seahawks waived him Tuesday.
With this addition, the Chargers essentially got a free sixth-round pick from the Seahawks. Joe Hortiz has not built a winning roster, but getting a sixth-round pick for free is a good addition to his resume.
With the addition of Smith, the Chargers depth chart will look to be:
CB1: Tarheeb Still CB2: Donte Jackson CB3: Cam Hart CB4: Deane Leonard CB5: Isas Waxter CB6: Avery Smith IR: Rodney Shelley
With Smith just coming back to the team, it should be expected for him to be relegated to special teams and reserve defensive roles, but in time, he could be promoted to as much as CB4, with the team obviously not loving what they have seen from Leonard and Waxter.
It should also be noted that Donte Jackson has been struggling mightily since his return from injury and if the team eventually fully commits to rebuilding, they could look to play the young DBs over a veteran on an expiring deal like Jackson.

title: 3 Things the Chargers Should be Thankful For This Thanksgiving
full_text:
The Los Angeles Chargers are 1-9; 2026 has been rough. Let's not pretend there is much for fans of the Chargers to be thankful for that is football-related this Thanksgiving, at least not in regards to the 2026 results.
The 2026 Chargers season has gone off the rails. All of the top players have been hurt at one point or another, the offensive line has been a constant game of musical chairs for the second season in a row and the offense has gone through multiple identity crises. But, the good news is, through the dark days of 2026, there have been several lighthearted moments and bits of news to find some thanks for Thanksgiving.
The Chargers' main connection to the fan base whether on social media platforms or content sources like YouTube is driven by one of if not the best social media team in the NFL. The time spent on schedule releases, fun videos and even post-game responses are fun and engaging.
To find a lighthearted moment, look no further than the announcement of Daiyan Henley's trade to the Broncos being followed up with the announcement the trade had been canceled. The reunion from the failed trade was going to be awkward for everyone and simply crossing out the "thank you" and handwriting "Welcome back" was a lighthearted twist from the social media team.
https://t.co/Ewbs7j6Yga pic.twitter.com/QzaZ40ZFF7
The Chargers may not be winning games but at least they still look good doing it. Despite the yellow uniforms still being around, at least when they debut later this season, the pants will be white instead of the full color rush style yellow.
ur favorite uniforms' favorite uniforms pic.twitter.com/O1QvxR0B3j
The silver lining with the terrible year on the field is that the Chargers will end up with a very high draft slot and pick high in every round in which they have their own picks. Going through a terrible season is not ideal but the top draft position does at least bring some level of hope for the future and the offseason ahead.
The Chargers are on track for a top three pick in the 2027 draft. Depending on where they ultimately pick, a draft slot that high can net a course-altering draft and in this upcoming class, all eyes will be on Ohio State wide receiver Jeremiah Smith.

title: Chargers' Joe Hortiz Pulls Off Savvy Move, Reacquiring Avery Smith
full_text:
Joe Hortiz brought Avery Smith back to the Chargers . This was a very smart decision , and it’s refreshing knowing Hortiz still can make the right moves.
Earlier in the season, the organization moved Smith and received a sixth-round draft pick. Now Smith is back, and the cost to reacquire him was no additional compensation. So essentially the Bolts got a free draft pick.
The original move brought a draft choice into the picture. A sixth-round selection may not sound like a major return, but every pick has value .
At the time, turning Smith into an extra selection gave the team another chance to add young talent.
The front office has recovered a player it knows while keeping the draft compensation it received earlier. The transaction gives the team a chance to benefit from both decisions , although the real value will depend on what Smith contributes.
I like the thinking behind this move because a roster decision does not always have to be permanent.
Teams make changes because of roster limits, immediate needs, player evaluations, and the value of draft picks. Circumstances can look different later. If a familiar player becomes available and still fits, bringing him back can be sensible.
There is no guarantee Smith will make a major impact. He still has to earn his place and turn this opportunity into production. The transaction itself does not promise playing time or success of course. Reacquiring him without spending another pick gives the coaching staff another option while protecting a future draft opportunity. That flexibility matters during a season. Injuries, performance, and changing roles can expose needs that were not obvious earlier. Another player can create competition and give the staff more choices when setting the lineup. Even if Smith’s role is limited, he could provide useful depth when it matters.
The next step belongs to Smith. He has a fresh chance to show he can help, while the team can evaluate whether the fit works this time. If he contributes, the organization may gain useful depth while holding on to the pick it collected earlier. If it does not work out, the team has not surrendered another selection to find out. That balance makes this reunion an interesting piece of roster management.
It is a reminder that roster building means recognizing when a previous decision can be revisited without paying twice for him again.
we’ve claimed CB avery smith off waivers → https://t.co/vrYHFtK8WQ pic.twitter.com/NSUceXhdsI
Brennan is sports writer focused on delivering sharp analysis, real-time reactions, and engaging storytelling focused on NFL analysis.  He is passionate about football and breaking down what matters to bring fans closer to the action.  Brennan comes from a family of Chargers fans.

title: Chargers Still Hoping Quentin Johnston Shakes Bust Label is Another Big Problem in LA
full_text:
It took a series of big missteps and overall mismanagement to put the Los Angeles Chargers in their current hole.
The weird misalignment between a thrifty front office and a poor coaching staff is a big part of it.
Look at former first-round pick Quentin Johnston.
The Chargers took Johnston in the first round back in 2023 and drop issues have been the major defining thing about his tenure, even overshadowing the fact he scored eight touchdowns apiece in 2024 and 2025.
Despite this, the Chargers and general manager Joe Hortiz took the obvious “bargain” by picking up Johnston’s fifth-year option.
Now 1-9, the Chargers have 15 catches for 275 yards and one touchdown from Johnston.
Let Chargers head coach Jim Harbaugh tell it, the offense just needs to get Johnston the ball more.
“We’ve got to get the ball to Quentin,” Harbaugh said . “I’d like to see the ball in Quentin’s hands. Blocked extremely well, but more targets, more opportunities, I think, would really help us. … You can’t force (targets) … but yeah, I’d like to see the ball in his hands more.”
It’s a pretty wild idea, considering Johnston has caught just 15 of his 32 targets. A Mike McDaniel offense that seems to need speedier options doesn’t really feel like it has a place for what Johnston brings to the table.
Making matters all the worse is that pesky fifth-year option. The Chargers are on the hook for a fully guaranteed $18 million salary next year. Nobody is walking through that door to trade for Johnston based on what he’s put on film.
So, looking ahead to 2027, what’s the play? Keep McDaniel and the bad fit? Start over with a coordinator who better fits a wideout who has caught 159 of 275 career targets from a quarterback like Justin Herbert? Let the $18 million player ride the bench?
The Chargers’ cheap front office isn’t helping. Johnston should be on an expiring contract right now, opening up their offseason options. It’s a problem that extends throughout the roster. They cheaped out on guards yet again and it shows. Not paying Odafe Oweh led to using a first-round pick on Akheem Mesidor when the answer was already on the roster. Don’t forget the “can’t-miss offer” for Daiyan Henley at the trade deadline to a rival after proclaiming they wouldn’t trade anyone, then failing that trade anyway.
Four seasons in now, Johnston’s time with the Chargers is pretty much up. Except, of course, for that pesky front office that values good deals more over actual production and winning. Until that front office proves otherwise, anyway.

title: Omarion Hampton is Perfect Example of Everything Wrong With Chargers
full_text:
Los Angeles Chargers running back Omarion Hampton is a fantastic football player.
The problem is, he plays for the Chargers.
Amid the 1-9 disaster, the Chargers boast emerging players to watch . Yet somehow, Hampton isn’t one of them, not really, because of a coaching and organizational approach that borders on malpractice.
Look right at the top with the listless Jim Harbaugh , who had some pretty shocking quotes about Hampton this week.
“Yeah, in hindsight, we should have done that sooner,” Harbaugh said . “I’m glad we’re doing it now, glad he’s certainly responded like the really good player that he is.”
Harbaugh was talking about making Hampton the workhorse back. He rushed for 105 yards and a score on 22 carries in a Week 10 win over Baltimore. He averaged 6.4 yards per carry on 14 chances in the loss to the New York Jets last week.
Before those games? Hampton was lost in a three-back rotation and he played fewer snaps than Kimani Vidal and Keaton Mitchell in weeks 4, 5 and 8. They went 0-8 over that span and are only just figuring out that Hampton might be the key.
How the heck did the Chargers get here?
Start back in 2025, when the Chargers decided that a running back was a good value in the first round at No. 22 overall. A wild decision, given the value debate around taking that position so early. And that’s to say nothing of the many premium spots on the offensive line, at wideout or across the defense they could have filled instead.
Hampton then struggled as a rookie at times due to injuries. He ended his rookie year with 124 carries, 545 yards and four scores on a 4.4 average over nine games. But the vision and obvious first-round stuff were there. The future was bright.
Then arrived Mike McDaniel this year and his weird insistence on running three-back looks. Keeping everyone fresh for the entire season is a nice idea, but when the record hits 0-5 or 0-6, maybe it’s time to step back and admit that making Hampton the workhorse everyone knows he can be might be the only way to pick up some wins.
That’s to say nothing of Joe Hortiz’s mediocre roster building. They knew the guard positions were an issue and signed an obvious dud in Cole Strange and had five guys competing for the other guard spot, including a second-round center Jake Slaughter asked to learn a new position in the pros.
It’s really just Chargering the whole thing. It was questionable to draft Hampton at all, they then failed to build the trenches in front of him properly, brought in a “good” coordinator who decided not to use him and are only just realizing near December that maybe the first-round running back should be playing more.
It would be funny if it weren’t so predictable and bordering on malpractice, really. Now, they’ll use Hampton as a workhorse in meaningless games, risk injury and top draft slotting the rest of the way, too.

title: Don’t Overlook These 3 Chargers Emerging Through Jets Loss
full_text:
The Los Angeles Chargers are 1-9 and coming off a loss at home to the New York Jets. The loss significantly moved the Chargers towards locking down a top-three pick in the 2027 draft but several players stood out in their efforts.
The Chargers are finally starting to get some consistency and players have carved out roles amidst injuries and the volatility associated with a 1-9 season. The Chargers will face significant questions heading into 2027 regarding roster construction and depth. Let's discuss three players who played or have been playing well enough to enter into 2027 considerations.
The Chargers have been featuring a heavy rotation of three edge rushers throughout most of the season with a fourth occasionally joining the mix. Veteran Bud Dupree has not played a snap on defense since week five with Caleb Murphy, now back with the Chargers for his second stint, taking over the role behind Khalil Mack, Tuli Tuipulotu and rookie Akheem Mesidor.
Murphy's role has slowly grown over the past few weeks and he had a monster sack negated by a penalty Sunday against the Jets. The play that was called back featured Murphy bull rushing the left tackle Olu Fashanu into Jets quarterback Geno Smith and Murphy reached through Fashanu to ensnare Smith and drag him to the ground along with the blocker.
Khalil Mack may not be back in 2027, and the Chargers and Tuli Tuipulotu have yet to come to terms on an extension leaving the edge rusher room thin heading into the offseason. Murphy, since returning to the Chargers, has shown significant development as an edge rusher as both a pass rusher and run defender. Paired with his effective play on special teams he should at the very least be considered a lock to be edge number four heading into next year.
Logan Taylor earned the starting left guard role, head coach Jim Harbaugh confirmed it during the week leading up to the Jets game. Taylor still has plenty of rookie wrinkles to smooth out but he has improved every week in the starting lineup. Taylor's ascension makes the rotation at left guard throughout training camp all the more confusing and frustrating in how that process played out only for it to naturally get figured out months later.
If Taylor can continue developing and head to the offseason with a solid foundation in the NFL, a full offseason of position-focused training, as opposed to combine preparation, should set him up to challenge for the starting job going forward.
Cole Strange: Unnecessary roughness Kayode Awosika: Very acceptable and necessary roughness pic.twitter.com/vUjTDZ9ovx
The Chargers signed Kayode Awosika this past offseason as a low-cost veteran guard to potentially compete for playing time in the reworked offensive line. He became the frontrunner for the starting left guard job almost instantly and despite the frustrating efforts of the coaching staff with questionable rotations, Awosika eventually won the starting job but was hurt with what was described as a fibula injury in week two against the Raiders, his only unopposed start before this past Sunday against the Jets.
Awosika was finally off the injury report following the Chargers victory over the Ravens and the Chargers plugged him into the starting lineup over Cole Strange who has been struggling. Inserting Awosika into the starting lineup immediately raised the floor of the unit and Awosika's physical presence helped rookie center Jake Slaughter and rookie tackle Travis Burke.
The Chargers will need to address their interior offensive line in the offseason and search for upgrades, but Awosika's presence should be strongly considered as an option to return to compete if he can stay healthy and keep performing down the stretch. The free agent guard class in 2027 may be light again and as history has shown, the Chargers need capable depth.

title: Justin Herbert Injury Updates: Latest on Chargers QB for Week 12 vs. Patriots
full_text:
Los Angeles Chargers quarterback Justin Herbert has a new injury to manage , this time ahead of his team’s Week 12 game against the New England Patriots.
After dealing with a finger issue in prior weeks, Herbert is now in concussion protocol.
Chargers head coach Jim Harbaugh told reporters early this week that Herbert “reported symptoms to the trainers and the doctors” after the loss to the New York Jets.
Here’s a look at Herbert injury updates before the Chargers play the Patriots in Week 12.
This story will be updated with more information as it becomes available .
At 1-9, the Chargers don’t have much hope without Herbert on the field. Primary backup Trey Lance is on injured reserve with an issue of his own.
Harbaugh provided a course of action if Herbert needs to miss Week 12: "Uiagalelei would be the next man up, and then we would bring Jake Browning up as well," Harbaugh said.
That’s DJ Uiagalelei, who has attempted seven passes this year, his only regular-season reps since entering the league. The Chargers also have Jake Browning on the practice squad, a journeyman backup who hasn’t attempted a regular-season pass since 2025.
At this point it should go without saying, but the Chargers and Mike McDaniel are a fantasy football disaster no matter who is out there. Herbert has completed 62.4 percent of his passes with eight touchdowns and 11 interceptions. His leading receiver has just 28 catches (Tre Harris) and lead back Omarion Hampton only just crept past the four-yards-per-carry mark on the season behind an offensive line battling various injuries.
With how things have gone, it’s now worth questioning whether the Chargers simply shut Herbert down for the season. But they certainly won’t rush him out there against the Patriots.

title: Jim Harbaugh’s Latest Stunning Moment Says It All About Chargers Future
full_text:
The Jim Harbaugh era sure feels like it’s over for the Los Angeles Chargers .
Before things hit 1-9 and the latest reason for Harbaugh’s firing went viral, it was easier to handwave this year as a fluke. It was even easy to argue that derailing Justin Herbert with yet another coaching staff would cause more problems when continuity might win the day.
But to say there are long-term concerns around the Chargers and Herbert now would be underselling things at this point.
And Harbaugh’s latest viral moment sort of points to where this whole thing is headed, for better or worse.
There are plenty of moments where outsiders could say “this is the one” in terms of the signs that things between Harbaugh and the Chargers had fully run their course.
But a rambling Harbaugh during a presser who didn't know what was going on with his own team just days prior is probably top of the list now.
Asked early this week which defensive player had the “green dot” on his helmet during the weekend’s loss to the New York Jets, Harbaugh stammered through a response and went as far as asking a background staffer for help with the question:
Reporter: “Who was wearing the green dot on Sunday” Jim Harbaugh: “I don’t know” then asks a staffer “Who had the green dot” Seems like something a head coach should know pic.twitter.com/POuXG8oHnw
First of all, it was a fair question. The failed Daiyan Henley trade and then an injury meant the starting linebacker didn’t have the green dot. Whether the communication duties went to another linebacker like Del’Shawn Phillips or Marlowe Wax is a very good question to ask.
The fact Harbaugh didn’t know? It’s concerning. After all, Harbaugh is a head coach, for starters. He’s also a “CEO” style coach who oversees the whole thing but really lets his coordinators do their thing.
Given this overarching responsibility, never mind the whole, you know, “head coach” thing, it’s eye-opening that Harbaugh doesn’t know which player was handling the communications to the sideline for one of his three units.
And considering we’ve been wondering if Harbaugh has lost the locker room already, it’s not a good sign for his usual “details matter” messaging in public to straight-up not know a detail like this.
Were the Chargers floating near even .500 before a sudden green dot change, this might not register as such a big deal. But adding it to the pile of a mess that is a 1-9 team and the fact this is another weird “checked out Harbaugh" moment and it looks terrible.

title: Chargers’ Jim Harbaugh Just Made the Best Case for His Own Firing Yet
full_text:
Exiting a rather embarrassing loss that sent them to 1-9, the Los Angeles Chargers don’t feel like a franchise that has any sense of direction yet when it comes to the fate of head coach Jim Harbaugh.
There’s a popular theory that Harbaugh’s contract will prevent the Chargers from moving on from him early. But that tends to overlook the fact the front office in Los Angeles has been willing to spend at times, whether it was actually paying up for Harbaugh, going to get Mike McDaniel or any other number of examples.
If the Chargers feel any hesitation on the Harbaugh topic though (hesitation would be ridiculous at 1-9, but hey), good news:
Harbaugh just made a pretty good case against his future employment during the latest loss.
It’s one thing to lose to the 3-8 New York Jets. The Chargers have looked like the worst team in football most weeks.
But it’s another to look completely lost in mid-November.
Alas, there was Harbaugh and his coaching staff on Sunday, seemingly in a position to really make a game of things in the fourth quarter.
Instead, inexplicable game management struck, as neatly summed up by Steven Haglund of the GAC Podcast:
The Chargers were down 10 points and really got down to the Jets 8 yard line with 4:33 left in the game and didn’t score until after the two minute warning today. After a 22 yard reception by Tre Harris gets them to that point: - Huddled, Herbert designed run at 3:50, loses 3…
One could almost accuse the Chargers of “tanking,” were it not for years of iffy game management by Harbaugh and his staff.
After the game, deja vu in the presser, too, with Harbaugh dropping his usual stuff. An example: "There's more work to be done, and we're going to work at it."
There were other examples, sure.
"We'll really look at the tape as it pertains offensively and see how we acquitted ourselves," Harbaugh said. "Some points of emphasis that got done, but if you don't win, everyone feels like there's more work to be done. Keep working at it."
And this is where it should dawn on onlookers that the Harbaugh way isn’t working. In the past, it was easier to overlook the in-game struggles and the cheesy one-liners because the locker room was bought in and winning (before the playoffs, anyway).
But now the message is lost. Bud Dupree’s tantrum aside, it sure feels like the Harbaugh message stopped working during last season’s playoff loss. Poor roster building and the injury bug haven’t helped things, but it’s pretty obvious it’s time for a refresh.
In fact, this is one of the better, more obvious examples of a franchise that needs an overhaul to the locker room by way of coaching staff change. And at this point, it’s almost worth wondering whether, if the Chargers front office won’t do it, Harbaugh himself might make it happen.

title: Chargers' Loss to Jets Raises Long-Term Concerns
full_text:
The Chargers lost yet another game, and it was quite embarrassing.
The Bolts took a 27-24 loss to the New York Jets, and it was not pretty at all. The offense looked decent compared to recent games, but the defense finally lost their touch .
The hope was to go up a winning streak, however that obviously didn't happen. In every game, there are players who perform better than others and that's just simply how it goes.
Hampton gave the Chargers a spark. He broke loose for a 36-yard run that helped set up a fourth-quarter scoring drive. That burst showed what the offense can look like when its ground game creates space.
Hampton did not score, but he found positive yardage and helped make the comeback possible. His production was a clear positive.
McConkey was the Chargers’ most important receiving threat near the goal line. He caught five passes for 37 yards, with two receptions going for touchdowns. Both scores came in the fourth quarter, keeping Los Angeles within striking distance. His yardage was modest, but finishing those drives mattered. When the Chargers needed a play, McConkey delivered twice. He was a bright spot in an offense that spent too much of the game searching for consistency.
Herbert found McConkey for two touchdowns and added a rushing score, helping keep the Chargers in the contest.
More troubling was the pressure. The Jets sacked him six times, disrupting drives and making it difficult to build momentum. Herbert avoided an interception, but Los Angeles cannot expect consistent results when its quarterback takes that many hits. He needed better protection and a stronger start.
The late scoring surge could not erase the earlier problems.
Johnston had too little impact when they needed more from its receivers. He caught one pass for nine yards on two targets and had one rushing attempt for a yard.
Those numbers did not give the offense much of a lift while the Chargers were trying to catch up. Johnston was not the only reason the passing game struggled, but the team needed another receiver to contribute alongside McConkey. His afternoon passed with barely a mark. The Chargers need more consistent production from him.
Njoku struggled to provide a spark.
The Chargers chased the game for long stretches, making each opportunity important. Njoku was not responsible for the defeat, but he offense needed more from its supporting cast to take pressure off McConkey. His limited production reflected a wider offensive problem: too many drives lacked an answer when the first option was covered.
Hampton’s running and McConkey’s touchdowns gave the Chargers something positive, but those moments could not cover the slow start or pressure allowed up front.
The Bolts scored 14 points in the fourth quarter, yet needed one more stop to complete the comeback. The Jets controlled the ball longer and finished with more total yards. A strong finish cannot substitute for a complete performance overall.
