title: Kyle Juszczyk Opens Up On When He Joined the 49ers Back in 2017
full_text:
San Francisco 49ers fullback Kyle Juszczyk is one of the oldest players on the roster, yet his decade-long stint in red and gold speaks volumes.
Juszczyk meets the criteria for what is considered a fan favorite . Not only has he been loyal to a franchise for over 10 years, but he has also earned this through his hard work, reliability, and consistent contributions to the team's success.
Juszczyk recalled joining the 49ers in free agency in 2017, the year Kyle Shanahan and John Lynch began their roles as head coach and general manager, respectively.
"What a different time. It felt like I was going to college again. I'd done my four years in Baltimore, which were like my college years, and now I was starting over again," said Juszczyk to NBC Sports Bay Area .
"It was a whole new regime, with a new head coach, new general manager and a whole new roster. I think we carried over about three players. It really was taking a chance and a risk by going to play with Kyle and trying to start something new and beautiful out here.
"Right away, meeting with Kyle and John, I knew these were the type of guys I wanted to go down that path with and start this journey alongside.
"It was really unique to be one of the very first players here and try to help lay the groundwork and foundation for what this organisation would look like for years to come."
Working with Shanahan for 10 years is something only he and George Kittle have achieved, giving him a core familiarity with how Shanahan galvanises the team to unleash their full potential. Juszczyk explained what makes Shanahan so special, highlighting his ability to motivate players, build strong relationships and bring out the best in everyone around him.
"What always resonated with me, probably because we're not that far apart in age, was his ability to connect with players on a youthful or friendship level, while also being an authority figure, a coach and a teacher," he added.
"He was always able to find that fine line between the two, and I think that's one of his greatest strengths as a coach."
And now Juszczyk will feature on the 49ers' 10-year wall, a historic moment for someone who arrived in his fifth season and then spent the next decade ( and maybe longer , though his contract expires this season) in San Francisco.

title: What the 49ers Can Expect from their Rookies in the Playoff Run
full_text:
The San Francisco 49ers have seven more games in the regular season and then a potential playoff run is coming. What are the expectations for the 2026 rookie draft class for the stretch run?
Stribling is supposed to return to practice around Week 14. So, he could return around Week 15 or 16. Even then, the room is now deep enough that he will likely just be a depth receiver.
Height is the 49ers fourth rusher. He is a depth option who is mostly a pass rusher. However, he ranks 10th in pass rush productivity and 11th in win rate amongst rookie edge rushers. The goal is for him to be more productive as a pass rusher.
Black has already exceeded expectations. However, the impact he has on McCaffrey has to remain. Black allows the 49ers to use McCaffrey in more beneficial ways without asking him to take on the tough carries.
Halton is out for the season due to an injury . Despite that, his rookie season will be viewed as a massive success due to the production he brought.
Willis is the backup left guard. Connor Colby has been rocky but not bad enough to warrant a benching. Still, he was the weak link on the line prior to the Colton McKivitz injury. There is a chance we see Willis at some point this year.
Injuries and the release of Jack Jones have pushed Prysock onto the field in a limited variety recently. The goal is for Prysock to continue to hold off Nate Hobbs for the third outside cornerback role. More than that, the 49ers trusting him in dime scenarios would help.
Dugger has done more than expected already. The goal for him is to be as good moving away from the football as he is when he is coming downhill towards the football. That is where Dugger is best.
The McKivitz injury opens the door for Cruz to play. However, all indications are that they want this year to be developmental.
The rookie UDFA has been a reliable option against the run. He just has to stay healthy and continue to hold down this role. The return of C.J. West could limit his snap counts down the stretch run.

title: The Teams that are Most Likely to Sign Former 49ers WR Brandon Aiyuk
full_text:
The unnecessary drama between Brandon Aiyuk and the San Francisco 49ers ended on Monday. Aiyuk has officially been cut and will look to sign with a new team. Let's explore the four teams he will likely sign with.
This is the team most likely to be interested in Aiyuk. He's been pining to join the Commanders all offseason, even making videos so far, even though he was already on the team.
There was a spat where Aiyuk and Jayden Daniels had a back-and-forth on social media in the Summer. But it seems it never went any deeper than that, as the two have reportedly mended fences .
Since there is no beef between them, signing Aiyuk is back on the table. With Terry McLaurin out for the season, the Commanders could use another receiver.
Stefon Diggs and rookie Antonio Williams aren't enough for them. Adding Aiyuk to form a trio could elevate their offense and give them a real shot at winning the NFC East after Week 11.
The most wide receiver depserate team in the league right now is the Los Angeles Rams. Star receiver Puka Nacua is most likely done for the season.
And there's no telling when Davante Adams will be back. Even if he returns in the next few weeks, the Rams can't have Adams as their only option. Aiyuk joining them makes perfect sense.
He goes into an offense that needs him and will funnel targets to him. That will boost his value in the offseason. Aiyuk also has the petty incentive of joining the 49ers' division rival. I'm sure that will be motivating.
Another team that Aiyuk can sign with for the petty incentive is the Seattle Seahawks. It won't be as good as the Rams since their quarterback and offense are whonky.
But he can still be a good fit since they need another receiver to complement Jaxon Smith-Njigba. Aiyuk would instantly be their No. 2 receiver, assuming he can come close to his level before his ACL tear.
Plus, offensive coordinator Brian Fleury knows him. He'll know how to get Aiyuk to fit and thrive in the offense. He should open things up as well.
Another desperate team that needs a wide receiver is the Las Vegas Raiders. They have no one noteworthy. Most of their targets go to their running backs and tight ends.
Rookie Fernando Mendoza needs a go-to receiver. Aiyuk can be that. Head coach Klint Kubiak is also familiar with Aiyuk from 2023, the year Aiyuk became an All-Pro.
If Aiyuk's social media behavior doesn't translate into the locker room, then he can help with Mendoza's development and provide a big boost to the Raiders' offense.

title: 49ers Could Face Tough Decision With Dominick Puni this Offseason
full_text:
One thing the San Francisco 49ers have not done under Kyle Shanahan and John Lynch is extend the interior offensive line. However, Dominick Puni is going to make their philosophy a lot tougher to stick to, according to Nick Wagoner of ESPN .
Wagoner called Puni the 49ers' clear extension candidate this offseason.
“Puni, who will be eligible for an extension for the first time this offseason, is the clear choice based on consistency and production,” wrote Wagoner.
The 49ers have not paid an interior lineman historically, but Puni might be the best option they have had so far. More than the 49ers' offensive line has a lot of long-term questions, making the team more apt to extend their guard to a big-money deal.
The 49ers have had a decent track record of letting linemen leave in free agency and then filling their hole without much issue.
They let Laken Tomlinson walk after 2021, and that might have been their biggest miss. He is still starting this year for the Green Bay Packers. Still, he has been on five teams since leaving San Francisco and has signed with four different teams in four different seasons after signing a big deal with the New York Jets.
Aaron Banks replaced Tomlinson in 2022. Now, Tomlinson has sent Banks to the bench two years into his big extension with the Packers. Green Bay regrets signing Banks.
The 49ers let Spencer Burford leave after starting at both guard spots. So far, Las Vegas has not been happy with his production. Tomlinson is the only potential miss, and even then the 49ers can say they felt good about letting him walk.
So, they could say that their philosophy has worked and they will stick to it. At the same time, Puni is the best interior lineman they have seen since Tomlinson, and he is likely a better option than him as well.
Puni is someone they drafted and developed. Beyond that, the age of Jake Brendel and Trent Williams, combined with the injury questions to Colton McKivitz, add instability to the line. They do not have a trusted left guard yet. So, Puni could be the one piece that the team builds around in the future.
Peter Skoronski set the market at $25M per year. With the way that Puni is playing, he will likely be approaching that number. Will the 49ers make the move?

title: Saints Coach Points to Bucs’ Bucky Irving When Asked About the Ideal RB
full_text:
The Tampa Bay Buccaneers have a crucial game against the Carolina Panthers on Monday.
The Bucs are two games out from the Carolina Panthers and can narrow the gap with a win, keeping them alive in the NFC South race. If they lose, though, their season could be over, and it would likely be because their passing offense is among the worst in the league.
The rushing offense, however, has been quite excellent. It's been spearheaded by Bucky Irving, who has been one of the league's best running backs. He's been the entire offense, and he may have to continue to be for the Bucs to stay in it.
Irving has drawn plenty of attention across the league — and that includes a coach on one of his biggest division rivals.
New Orleans Saints running backs coach Joel Thomas said on a recent appearance with the Senior Bowl that he's been watching some film of Irving lately — and that Irving is the exact type of running back he's looking for whenever he's scouting players.
"I like that chip, I like that edge, I like that tough guy mentality when you're playing that position," Thomas said. "I'm watching Bucky Irving playing against Chicago. And he is a dog," Thomas said. "The he way he runs, it's relentless. It's 'I'm full-go, I'm going to get this first down. I'm not going down first contact.' Those are the type of guys that we're looking for and that we're training."
What does Saints RB coach Joel Thomas look for in a running back? There’s a certain back playing for a division rival who checks those boxes 👀 #TheDraftStartsInMobile pic.twitter.com/Mozb4m3bog
The compliment is a kind one from a division rival, but when you look at the numbers, it's not hard to see why he might admire Irving as opposed to his own players.
Quarterback Tyler Shough is the Saints' leading rusher, believe it or not, with 221 rushing yards. Running back Travis Etienne Jr. is the second-best rusher at 218 yards on the year, and the Saints are averaging 93.1 yards per game on the ground — the 28th-best number in the NFL.
Irving, meanwhile, has been a phenom this year. He's put up 893 yards for 4.8 yards per carry and eight rushing touchdowns, on pace for the best season of his career. He ran for 170 yards against the Atlanta Falcons and 165 against the Dallas Cowboys, both games coming close to Shough's entire rushing total this year.
In that case, divisional envy makes a lot of sense. And Thomas won't have to wait too long to watch Irving in person.
The Bucs and Saints square off in Week 15 on Dec. 20 before playing each other to end their seasons (the regular season, at least) in Week 18 at a time to be determined. The NFC South remains close, with the Bucs and Saints both two games out from the Carolina Panthers.
We'll see if those matchups end up holding real weight later in the season. For now, though, Thomas will have to keep admiring Irving from afar on film.

title: Bucs Coach Named Potential Candidate for Glenn Schumann's FSU Staff
full_text:
The state of Florida has an illustrious history when it comes to the game of football.
The Miami Dolphins and the Tampa Bay Buccaneers each have two Lombardi Trophies, and the likes of the big three college teams — Florida State, Florida and Miami — have plenty of National Championships of their own.
However, the Seminoles of Florida State have struggled lately, ultimately leading to the firing of Mike Norvell and the hiring of Glenn Schumann as the next head coach.
With Schumann's hiring, he will be putting together a staff, and one Buccaneers' coach is being tabbed as a potential hire.
"McClendon has a vast background coaching receivers, working at Georgia, South Carolina, and Oregon, prior to leaping to the NFL in 2024. He was the wide receivers coach and pass-game coordinator for the Bulldogs in 2022-23, spending two seasons alongside Schumann," OnSI's Dustin Lewis wrote .
"The Buccaneers could make a coaching change, with the franchise on pace to miss the postseason for the second straight year. If so, McClendon will be looking for a new job. FSU would probably have to throw a co-OC title, at a minimum, to lure him back to college."
As mentioned by Lewis, McClendon came into the Bucs' organization in 2024, becoming a part of one of the most lucrative offenses in recent team memory under Liam Coen.
McClendon has become known as a player-first, no-ego coach who has blended young talent with veteran presence since his arrival in Tampa Bay.
Despite a lack of experience at the NFL level, McClendon is highly regarded in NFL and collegiate circles, and he has been challenged throughout his NFL tenure by a lack of consistency from players missing time due to injury.
Even though McClendon has done a fantastic job during his short time with the Bucs, things have taken a nosedive for his unit in 2026 following the departure of Mike Evans and the lack of development from players like Emeka Egbuka.
Depending on how the rest of the season pans out for Tampa Bay, McClendon could see this as an opportunity to head back to the college ranks and join coach Schumann in Tallahassee.
If McClendon were to leave and head to Florida State this offseason, it would set him up as a prime candidate to receive a promotion to offensive coordinator in the future.
As for the impact on the Bucs, it would be a shot to a group that has seen success under McClendon and leave them searching for a replacement on top of a likely change at offensive coordinator of their own.

title: Positive Signs Emerge at Buccaneers’ Wednesday Practice
full_text:
The Tampa Bay Buccaneers are still trying to win the NFC South and make the playoffs. But for all intents and purposes, their Week 12 game on Monday Night Football is a playoff game already.
The Bucs face off against the Carolina Panthers on Monday Night Football. The Panthers have a two-game lead in the division at 5-5, while the Bucs sit at 3-7. If the Bucs beat the Panthers, they sweep Carolina and move within one game of the division — lose, and their playoff chances are almost certainly over three games back.
The Bucs will need everyone they can muster to help win that game. And the good news is that they could have some crucial players for that contest.
Cornerback Jacob Parrish was back at practice on Wednesday after leaving the game with a back injury on Sunday. Parrish was replaced by Benjamin Morrison, who was also injured in that game — Morrison was not at practice, but Parrish was.
Parrish has been one of the best corners in football this season, netting 14 passes defended and two interceptions so far this year. He's a crucial part of the defense, so having him will be important.
Perhaps the bigger story, however, is that wideout Jalen McMillan began his 21-day practice window. McMillan injured his knee in the preseason and had a procedure to rectify it, but he re-injured that knee during Tampa Bay's Week 2 game against the Cleveland Browns. He's been out since then, but now, he could return as soon as Monday.
McMillan isn't guaranteed to be back. But if he is, he'd be very valuable — Tampa Bay's wide receiver corps has been very lackluster so far this season. McMillan has been strong against man coverage and is a good separator when he plays, so the Bucs could really use his skill set as soon as possible.
The Bucs will play the Panthers at 8:15 p.m. on Monday. Whether or not Parrish or McMillan plays remains to be seen, but it's very encouraging to see them at practice.

title: Todd Bowles Says Buccaneers Are 'Running Out of Time'
full_text:
It might appear that the Tampa Bay Buccaneers 2026 season is a loss when you look at their 3-7 record, but they are still in the playoff mix as they sit just two games back of the NFC South lead with an all-important prime time matchup against the Carolina Panthers on deck.
There have been positives and negatives to take away from how the Bucs have performed this season, but head coach Todd Bowles doesn't believe that it's one thing — or even a couple — that is keeping this team from having a better record through 10 games.
“It’s few more than one or two things, but you know, the effort is not even a question,” Bowles said on Movin’ The Chains on SiriusXM NFL Radio . “The guys’ gonna fight every week. It’s just about cleaning up the little things and it’s the guy here or there and, you know, we’re running out of time... You know, you gotta correct those things.”
Bowles isn't wrong in his statement. The players have been fighting their tail off, but it has come to no avail.
However, it is worrisome that even Bowles is noticing that the Bucs haven't been able to take care of the little things, given the point of the season we are in.
But one thing is for sure — the Bucs are running out of time, and they must have a fire lit under them to finish the season strong if they hope to make the postseason.
Being just two games out of first place in the division should be motivation enough to go out there and get it right. On top of that, Tampa Bay has one of the easiest schedules remaining, with games against the Panthers, the Los Angeles Rams, the Los Angeles Chargers, the New Orleans Saints and the Atlanta Falcons, who have a combined winning percentage of just .333.
Things are lining up for the Bucs to win the majority of their remaining games, but they must make sure everything is buttoned up in order to do so.
They will have to battle injuries and somehow figure out how to improve their passing game if they hope to rip off a winning streak.
There is minimal room for error for this Bucs team, but they clearly are better than their record shows. If they want to hush the doubters and turn things around, they will need to get the little things right the rest of the way.

title: This Buccaneers Rookie is Turning Heads in 2026
full_text:
The Tampa Bay Buccaneers defense has been the strong suit of the team this season, the opposite of what we thought heading into the season.
The likes of Zyon McCollum and Jacob Parrish have been the big players on defense, but as a whole, the unit has exceeded expectations, becoming one of the top defenses in the league through the midway point of the season.
One player in particular has taken the bull by the horns — rookie linebacker Josiah Trotter.
Trotter has gone vastly unnoticed in his rookie season, mainly due to the Bucs underwhelming on the season. However, he is now starting to get the attention he rightfully deserves.
NFL analyst Ben Fennell took to X to point out how well Trotter has been playing and highlighting his natural instincts, particularly against the run.
Bucs Josiah Trotter is one of the most gifted rookie LBs I've ever seen/studied. 21 years old lol Dude has an insanely quick/confident trigger on his run reads... but isn't ever out of control - feels run action so so well. pic.twitter.com/ueuA95kTmj
Fennell's post made it's way around the web, and led to others chiming in on Trotter.
"Bucs are so bad he probably isn’t getting the attention he deserves, but he’s right up there behind Reese for DROY runner up imo," NFL analyst Jon Ledyard posted .
CBS Sports' JP Acosta also chimed in — "Real ones knew."
There were worries about Trotter's game when he was selected in the NFL Draft by the Bucs, but he has since quelled all worries since taking over as a full-time starter for the defense.
Trotter has been one of the best linebackers in the league against the run and has also shown great promise as a blitzer, creating pressure in the backfield. He has also improved drastically from his collegiate days when it comes to securing tackles, only being knocked for six missed tackles on the season.
He is also the only rookie defender to have a pick-six.
All signs point towards Trotter having a great career in the NFL with how he has performed so far, but he will have to improve in certain areas, most notably when it comes to coverage in space.
Trotter has been performing well up to the levels of Arvell Reese and Jacob Rodriguez, with Sonny Styles and Anthony Hill Jr. also performing above expectations early in their careers.
The 2025 linebacker class is looking like one of the best in quite some time, and for Trotter to be a part of that means the Bucs have a good one for years to come.

title: This Stat is a Huge Reason Why Baker Mayfield Has Been Struggling
full_text:
The Tampa Bay Buccaneers ' offense has struggled all year. The run game has been a success, but the passing game is among the league's worst and has hurt Tampa Bay week in and week out.
There are a lot of reasons why the offense is struggling. The play calling has been lackluster from offensive coordinator Zac Robinson, and the lack of talent in the wide receiving corps has made facilitating the passing game quite difficult. A big part of the equation, however, is quarterback Baker Mayfield.
Mayfield — whom the Bucs extended on a three-year, $55 million per year deal this offseason — has played very poor football dating back to the latter half of 2025. There are plenty of reasons for that, with injuries and decision-making being key factors, but there's another huge reason why he's struggled this year.
When Mayfield gets pressured by opposing defenses, he tends to get sacked. And that kills Tampa Bay's offense.
Sacks are not solely the fault of the offensive line. They certainly play a role, but sacks are just as much a quarterback stat as they are an offensive line stat — maybe even more so.
If the quarterback gets the ball out in good rhythm, he will naturally avoid sacks. That includes throwing it to receivers and throwing the football away, and obviously, it also accounts for mobility in the pocket and shedding rushers. Sacks are incredible swings in the defense's favor — the more a quarterback can avoid them of his own volition, the better the entire offense is.
Pressure-to-sack ratio, then, asks how often a quarterback is sacked when he is pressured. Good quarterbacks avoid getting sacked when pressured, either by getting the ball out or evading the defender. It's an important stat to gauge how long a quarterback holds the ball and how often he is costing the offense by going down.
Baker Mayfield, historically, is very, very bad at this. This year, he's 34th of 34 quarterbacks in pressure-to-sack ratio, getting sacked on 22 of his 80 pressured dropbacks, per SumerSports (27.5%). His best year since 2022 was 2025, when his 15.5% was ranked 16th of 45, but in that same time span, he's had seasons ranked 42nd of 46 (2024, 23.5%) and 44th of 47 (2022, 26.7%).
If you look cumulatively since 2022, he's ranked 63rd of 88 among quarterbacks with at least 100 dropbacks (20.5%). If you narrow that further and only go from quarterbacks with a comparable number of dropbacks to Mayfield — within 25% either way of his 2,509 dropbacks since 2022 — he's dead last, 19th of 19 quarterbacks.
This problem has plagued Mayfield his entire career. It's a big reason why he's been able to excel with strong coordinators, but when he's dealing with worse situations in coaching and the team's wide-receiving talent, he's unable to elevate the offense by himself as a player.
Perhaps the worst part of this equation is that Mayfield is 31 years old and is playing in his ninth NFL season. This aspect of the game gets less and less fixable every year he's in the league — this is simply who he is, and it's a major negative aspect of his game that anyone starting him has to deal with.
Right now, that team is the Bucs. They committed to Mayfield before the offseason with a three-year, $55 million extension, and after a better year on this front last year, he's regressed back to his usual ways.
Mayfield is currently dealing with a foot injury, which makes his mobility tougher than it would be when healthy. He moved around well in Detroit, but he still took a few sacks, including a strip sack and a crucial sack on fourth-and-12 to essentially end the game.
The Bucs play the Panthers on Monday night at 8:15. Mayfield will have to find ways to avoid going to the ground, because if he doesn't, this passing offense will continue to suffer.

title: Buccaneers Could Be in Serious Trouble After Two Players Need MRIs
full_text:
The Tampa Bay Buccaneers play arguably the most important game of the season on Monday night when they face off against the Carolina Panthers — a win keeps them alive in the NFC South, and a loss almost certainly ends their season.
Bad news for the Bucs? They might have a very, very thin secondary for that matchup.
Defensive back Jacob Parrish left the Detroit game early with a back injury, and he was replaced by cornerback Benjamin Morrison. Morrison gave up two touchdowns during the game, but he also injured his hamstring and had to leave as well.
Head coach Todd Bowles gave an update on both players on Monday, and it seems the injuries are at least worrisome enough that they need to get second looks.
Bowles confirmed on Monday that both Parrish and Morrison are getting MRIs to gauge the severity of their injuries.
"They're both getting MRIs today, so we'll have a better update later this afternoon," Bowles said.
The results of those MRIs won't be known until Wednesday, but the Bucs will have been hoping to get some good news. Parrish has been one of the best cornerbacks in football this year, and while Morrison struggled against Detroit, he provides good depth for the team in case of an emergency and has played well in spurts prior to that game this year.
So who's next if both aren't healthy? It's Kevin Knowles, who was brought in this offseason to play special teams. Behind him will have to be either Ayden Garnes, an undrafted free agent who made the team this offseason, or Josh Hayes, a veteran Bucs player who is still on injured reserve and in the middle of his 21-day practice window.
Either way, losing just one of Parrish or Morrison would be unfortunate, given the importance of the Panthers game next Monday. Parrish is the crucial player, though, so it will be interesting to see if he practices on Wednesday ahead of the Monday matchup.
The Bucs play the Panthers at 8:15 on Monday Night Football.

title: Buccaneers Play Most Important Game of Their Season Next Week
full_text:
The Tampa Bay Buccaneers are no strangers to pressure or to the prime-time lights. They've won their division close in a few of Todd Bowles' seasons as head coach, and they've had to play in prime time plenty.
On Monday, they'll face both. The Bucs play the division-leading Carolina Panthers at home on Monday Night Football, and it comes after Bowles and the Bucs lost their Week 11 game against the Detroit Lions to fall to 3-7 on the year.
The game is not just important. It's arguably the most important game the Bucs will play all year, and that's something the coaching staff knows as well.
With the Atlanta Falcons' bye week, the NFC South is now all caught up on games played. And after winning two games in a row, the Carolina Panther are two games out from the entire rest of the field.
Simply put, this game against the Panthers is the singular most-important game the Bucs will have all year. A win puts Tampa Bay within one game of the NFC South lead and gives them the ultimate tiebreaker over the Panthers — if Tampa Bay can keep it close for the rest of the year, they'll hold the match point over Carolina at season's end.
Lose, though? The Panthers will be three games out from Tampa Bay, and the two will have split the series, eliminating that tiebreaker for the Bucs. If the Panthers emerge victorious on Monday Night Football, Tampa Bay's season is as good as over at 3-8.
The Bucs know that. Bowles said as much on Monday.
"Yeah, [the players are] aware of it. They understand," Bowles said. "They know where we stand. It starts with us in this room, so we've got to correct everything and turn that thing around. We've got to do it a game at a time."
The Bucs' entire playoff hopes hinge on this game. And if Tampa Bay doesn't win it, any hope Bowles has of retaining his job as head coach is probably gone, too, so he'll really be looking to win this game on Monday night.
Things went well for the Bucs last time they played Carolina on the road. Will it be the case at home? If Tampa Bay wants to stay alive, it simply must be.

title: Bucs' Best Pass Rusher Played Just 19 Snaps, and Todd  Bowles' Explanation Is Concerning
full_text:
The Tampa Bay Buccaneers lost their game to the Detroit Lions 31-21 in a game that wasn't as close as the score makes it seem. The offense struggled mightily in all respects, and while the defense did their job for most of the game, some lapses allowed the Lions to put up some big points.
It wasn't all doom and gloom for the Bucs, though. One of their second-year players in his first NFL season, David Walker, has been shining, and he currently leads the team both in pressure rate and with sacks — he has five on the year.
Despite that, though, Walker isn't getting a lot of playing time. He only played 19 snaps on Sunday despite getting the team's only sack and making a big special teams play, and he was outsnapped by Yaya Diaby, Rueben Bain Jr. and Anthony Nelson on the day.
Head coach Todd Bowles was asked about why Walker's snap count was so low, and his answer was certainly an interesting one.
"Yeah, based off personnel yesterday, obviously, with that being more of a running team and putting bigger guys in there, we needed bigger guys on the field," Bowles said. "But David is a big part of everything we're doing. We love him to death, and he actually played the run well. He can get engulfed sometimes because of size, and you've got to be careful of that, but as he gets the system down more, he plays more and more. We love everything he's doing."
It is true that Walker is a bit smaller for an outside linebacker, and it's also true that Detroit has been very successful running behind running back Jahmyr Gibbs.
But Walker's pressure rate is arguably worth much more than potential size problems at the edge, and the Lions' passing offense excelled without much pressure coming it way — quarterback Jared Goff completed 71.4% of his passes for 279 yards and two touchdowns on the day, and Walker could have really been needed there.
There are also other smaller players who struggle against the run and who played much more than Walker did. Defensive tackle Calijah Kancey, who is notably undersized himself, played 30 snaps on the day — 52% of all defensive snaps.
Walker also had nine total pass reps on the day. Of those nine pass reps, he spent three of them dropping back in coverage, so those are more snaps where he isn't involved in pressuring the quarterback.
Walker has proved that, at least this season, he is the team's best pass rusher. He may be undersized, but he should be on the field far, far more often, and he's certainly done enough to prove it over these first 10 games in Tampa Bay.
The Bucs play the Carolina Panthers on Monday night. It will be interesting to see whether or not Walker gets more snaps.

title: Todd Bowles Gives Explanation For Crucial Part of Loss to Lions
full_text:
The Tampa Bay Buccaneers didn't just lose one way in their 31-21 defeat to the Detroit Lions. They faltered on offense, defense and in coaching, and that all created the environment to bring the Bucs down to 3-7.
There was one specific issue, however, that fans and pundits alike noticed across the game, and it cost the Bucs dearly throughout the entire contest.
The Bucs had two delay-of-game penalties because they were unable to get the play off in time. Additionally, multiple other plays saw the Bucs leave the huddle with 10 or less seconds remaining — this included a crucial 4th & 12, which resulted in a sack as the team hurried to get the play off.
This has been a problem all year, but it was particularly noticeable against the Lions on Sunday.
Head coach Todd Bowles spoke on Monday after the loss, and when asked about this specific issue, he didn't have a particularly thorough answer.
"It's a combination of everything," Bowles said Monday. "We gotta get out of the huddle quicker, we gotta get to the line quicker, we gotta put the play in quicker. It's a combination of everything."
That answer doesn't clear up the problem, and leads one to wonder what exactly has been happening with this issue across the season so far.
The most likely culprit is that offensive coordinator Zac Robinson is getting the play calls in too late, which causes the offensive operation to slow down. There is a chance that quarterback Baker Mayfield is having trouble relaying the play, but his job is generally to repeat what Robinson is saying through the headset. If the Buccaneers aren't getting to the line fast enough, as Bowles said, too, that could also be a personnel issue with players not knowing where to go once the huddle breaks.
No matter how it's spun, these are typically things that work themselves out in preseason and training camp, and the fact that the Bucs are struggling with this in Week 11 is a rough look.
If the play call comes in late, the offensive operation is completely thrown off. Mayfield needs time to read the defense and make protections, and if the clock is winding down, he has less time to do that. Additionally, pre-snap motion takes time to develop, and that aspect has to be rushed as well if the play isn't in quickly enough.
The Bucs play the Carolina Panthers on Monday Night Football. If they lose that game, their playoff hopes will be all but dashed, so they'll want to fix this issue — and many others — ahead of that game.

title: Could Titans Draft Their RB of the Future With a Second-Round Steal in 2027?
full_text:
In the 2026 NFL Draft, the Titans took LB Anthony Hill Jr. in the second round. Hill came onto the scene as a promising defensive prospect from the jump, but it took no time at all for him to blossom into a bonafide defensive star. He's Tennessee's tackle leader, and already looks like a long-term stud.
I'm here today to posit a scenario where the Titans repeat that second-round luck in 2027, but on the opposite side of the ball. With one of their two second-rounders, Tennessee should be kicking the tires on Boise State RB Dylan Riley.
The Broncos' Ashton Jeanty replacement has quietly had an elite season as a junior. The springy, multi-tool weapon is being overshadowed by other players at his position, but if anything, that would allow the Titans to steal an already underrated prospect off the board.
For Tennessee to end up with one of Jadan Baugh or Kewan Lacy, the two top RBs in 2027, they'd likely have to consider burning their later first-round pick. With as many defensive needs as the Titans have, as well as the near-guarantee of taking WR Jeremiah Smith at first overall if Tennessee keeps that pick, loading up with an RB that early doesn't seem feasible.
The door is wide open, however, in the second round. That's right where Riley falls. The Boise State back comes in at 42nd on ESPN's 2027 big board, and Bleacher Report even has him slated as their RB2 in the class.
Naturally, competing in the Pac 12 (the new one, at that) means Riley isn't facing SEC-caliber defenses on a weekly basis. But Riley has strengths that should translate to the NFL, and the Titans should have him circled as a quality succession plan for Tony Pollard for that reason.
At 5-foot-10, 192 lbs, Riley's game is all about his quickness and ability to make defenders miss. He's got a varied move-set (including a hurdle, pictured above) and the ability to explode through gaps and footrace opponents to the end zone .
This season, Riley has 213 carries for 1,360 yards (sixth in the nation). That's 6.4 yards per carry to go along with his 11 rushing touchdowns. Riley also has 25 receptions for 317 yards and two extra scores.
Riley's skillset has prepared him for the jump to the NFL, and for Tennessee, you couldn't ask for a more compelling pick past the first round. If Pollard and Spears both go in free agency, the RB1 role will likely fall on the shoulders of a rookie.
Given the team's needs and general offensive makeup, I believe Dylan Riley has a great case to be that rookie.
Lane covers the Tennessee Titans, where he brings an evolving team's journey to fans on a daily basis. A longtime sports fanatic and recent baby blue jersey aficionado.

title: 4 Things the Titans Should Be Thankful For This Thanksgiving — No Current Player Takes the Top Spot
full_text:
If you're reading this before you chow down on some Thanksgiving turkey with friends and family, don't let your favorite 1-9 football team bog down the holiday spirit today. There's always something to be thankful for, even with the Tennessee Titans.
In fact, if you look at things the right way, there's a lot to smile about in Nashville. Maybe not a full, toothy smile, but a corner-mouth grin. A smile is a smile all the same.
Here's my ranking of four things the Titans should be thankful for this Thanksgiving, upcoming divisional brawl and all.
If you can't find much to be happy about right now, look to the horizon. The Titans have an absurdly exciting draft outlook over the next two seasons.
The team's deadline trades hampered their current efforts, but the Titans now have two first-round and second-round picks in 2027 and 2028. Not only that, but Tennessee currently holds the first overall pick next spring, which would likely yield generational WR Jeremiah Smith.
Rookies and second-year players make up the beating heart of this Titans team. Youth is the name of the game in Nashville right now, and that will only become more true in the years to come.
Cam Ward might not take the top spot, but Tennessee should be thrilled with their QB's recent development.
Over the past three weeks of football, Ward has thrown just one interception to six touchdowns. He's performing well in an offense progressively suited to his strengths and just returned rookie sensation Carnell Tate to the lineup - more on Tate later.
Ward has safely moved into the middle of the pack of NFL signal callers, and is still steadily climbing. He's not perfect, but questions about his potential benching have been long forgotten. For now, at least, the Titans don't have a question under center.
That's worth a plate of celebratory seconds.
In the same vein as Ward's success, Tennessee should be singing the praises of their turn to the no-huddle offense today.
Brian Daboll's move to this system in Week 8 (when the Titans eclipsed 40% usage for the first time this season) directly coincided with the offense's first 30+ point game of the year. Per Sharp Football Analysis, the Titans' no-huddle rate on the year is up to 25.3%.
That's comfortably the highest in the NFL. If it ain't broke don't fix it, especially not after it was broken for the first five games of the season. Daboll has found a balance, and he should keep feeding it throughout the rest of this year.
Finally, I'd be remiss not to mention Tennessee's mostly outstanding rookie class. EDGE Keldric Faulk looks to be an unfortunate exception, but today is not the day to pick that wound.
The aforementioned Tate, as well as LB Anthony Hill Jr., each secured rookie of the month honors from the NFL this season. RG Fernando Carmona Jr., before being sent to IR after Week 3, came in as a surprise starter on the offensive line.
No draft is flawless, but general manager Mike Borgonzi reeled in multiple quality rookies this past spring. Between these guys and the draft picks the Titans have, it may be the truth that no team in the league has as much promise on this front as Tennessee.
What isn't exciting now can be exciting later. Borgonzi has the tools to get this franchise out of the mud as early as next season. To the Titans fans that celebrate: Have a happy Thanksgiving, and don't be afraid to revel in what this team could become with a few more well-picked rookies.

title: 3 Titans Developments Fans Should be Watching Weekly as 2026 Season Winds Down
full_text:
Over the offseason, Tennessee Titans' GM Mike Borgonzi introduced Robert Saleh as the franchise's next head coach and approached free agency aggressively, spending more than $265 million with hopes of dawning a success era in Nashville. They even debuted new threads with the color palette paying homage to their predecessor, the Houston Oilers, with a modern twist ahead of their final season in Nissan Stadium.
However, the Titans find themselves sitting at the bottom of the NFL standings at a 1-9 record, in the same spot they were last season only weeks after firing their head coach, Brian Callahan.
Tennessee has underperformed beyond the expectations of pundits, fans, and the coaching staff in what has been one of the most challenging seasons in franchise history. “These last couple of weeks, I'm not gonna try to sugarcoat anything," Saleh said to the media this week . "It's been dog----."
There's little to be optimistic about for Titans' fans. Nonetheless, there are still eight games remaining on the schedule that will impact the future of the franchise. While Tennessee may not win another game for the remainder of the season, here are three developments every Titans fan should keep an eye on.
The Titans are currently in possession of the No. 1 pick in the upcoming 2027 NFL Draft.
Unlike other professional sports leagues that use a lottery system to determine draft order, the NFL assigns the top pick to the team with the fewest wins. Tennessee edges out fellow one-win teams, the Los Angeles Chargers and the Miami Dolphins, due to the Titans facing a greater strength of schedule .
The Titans have an opportunity to secure the number one pick if they continue to lose. Later this season, the Chargers and Dolphins will face off, which could help Tennessee keep the top spot. Looking ahead at the Titans' schedule, they play Jacksonville, Washington, Detroit, Indianapolis, Las Vegas, Pittsburgh and Houston.
Each of the Titans' opponents are looking to win because they're either in the playoff picture or in the hunt. Even the lowly 3-8 Colts, because the Jets have ownership of their first-round pick.
Another important draft contingent for Tennessee is the Chicago Bears. The midseason Jeffery Simmons deal included a first-round draft pick in 2027, which will likely be a late-round pick because the Bears have an 8-2 record.
However, the pick still has a chance to fall because the Bears play in the highly competitive NFC North, with every team having at least six wins. Chicago has one more game against each NFC North rival remaining on their schedule.
Following a loss to the Houston Texans 26-3 in Week 5, the buzz around QB Cam Ward peaked. At that game in Nissan Stadium, Titans' fans were holding up signs mocking the young quarterback. However, Ward has helped turn Tennessee into the sixth-highest scoring offense in the NFL since Week 8, according to StatMuse .
In the month of November, Ward has thrown for 783 yards, scored seven touchdowns and only one interception on an efficient 68.8% completion percentage across three games. For two of those games Ward was without his No. 1 target, WR Carnell Tate, and a game-and-a-half without WR Wan'Dale Robinson, the WR2.
Without a doubt, the second-year quarterback has been playing the best football of his pro career. Ward's improved play lifts pressure off the shoulders of the Titans' front office.
Tennessee shouldn't spend a second- or third-day draft selection on a potential replacement or feel tempted to spark a desperate trade for an aging veteran. Instead, the front office should focus on improving a Tennessee defense that has allowed almost 45 points per game in the last three games.
Week-to-week Ward has been improving and finding a rhythm regardless of who's on the field for the Titans. In November, Ward's six touchdown throws have been to six different receivers. Titans' fans should be encouraged by Ward's recent uptick in production and have more optimism about their young quarterback heading into next season.
As previously mentioned, Ward has found six different receivers in the end zone this month; half of those targets are age 25 or younger. Robinson is 25, Tate is 23, and WR Chimere Dike is 24. Although he hasn't scored this month, WR Elic Ayomanor's 140 receiving yards is the second-highest number of receiving yards of any Titan in November. He's only 23 years old in his second season.
Tennessee's depth at receiver has been pivotal for Ward's development. The next-man-up mentality when Tate and Robinson have missed time with injuries has allowed Dike and Ayomanor a chance to prove themselves as reliable receivers.
Prior to his injury in Week 7 against Cleveland, Tate was the favorite to win AP Offensive Rookie of the Year. Still, despite missing two-and-a-half games this season, Tate is second in receiving yards and receiving touchdowns and fifth in receptions amongst all rookies this season, according to StatMuse .
Tate has the shot at becoming the first Titan to win the award since Vince Young in 2006. Currently, Tate has the third-best odds to win on DraftKings, only behind Broncos' RB Jonah Coleman and Raiders' QB Fernando Mendoza, per ESPN .
If the Titans lock in the top pick in the 2027 NFL Draft, the front office will have an opportunity to add to Tennessee's offensive firepower by selecting the consensus No. 1 pick, Ohio State WR Jeremiah Smith.
He's widely considered a generational talent. Smith is the most hyped receiver coming out of college since Calvin Johnson, who was selected No. 2 in 2007 by the Detroit Lions and later became a first-ballot Hall of Famer.
Whether or not Smith joins Tate and Ward in Nashville, there's already significant talent to build on in the future.
Isaiah is an award-winning journalist and photojournalist. A graduate from the University of Kentucky, he has previously been published by BloodHorse, KY Insider, and the Kentucky Kernel for multimedia sports coverage. Isaiah is a Tennessee Volunteer at heart bringing his local expertise to Titans coverage.

title: How 1 Underrated Signing is Redeeming Titans' Free Agency Pickups From 2026 Offseason
full_text:
The Tennessee Titans were one of the most active teams in NFL free agency this past offseason, as the team invested big money in premium positions, including wide receiver with Wan'Dale Robinson, defensive tackle with John Franklin-Myers, and cornerback with Alontae Taylor.
Robinson is on IR, Taylor has had perhaps the worst season of his career, and Myers was left virtually alone on the defensive line after the Jeffery Simmons trade. The outlook is bleak.
However, one signing that flew a bit under the radar was center Austin Schlottmann, whom the Titans signed to a two-year deal worth up to $9 million . Schlottmann began his career with the Denver Broncos, and also had two-year stints with the Minnesota Vikings and New York Giants.
Entering 2026, Tennessee was banking on Schlottmann providing serviceable center play and helping anchor the offensive line to an improved season. So far, he's done that and has been a bright spot on a unit that has endured its fair share of ups and downs.
Is Schlottmann an elite interior offensive lineman? No. But the veteran has quietly been a solid piece of the Titans' offensive line and is making the case to be the starting center for another year.
Through 10 starts this season, Schlottmann has allowed just one sack and 12 quarterback pressures, earning a 64.3 Pro Football Focus pass-blocking grade . Though he is leaving a lot to be desired in the run game, posting a 53.2 run-blocking grade, Schlottmann is coming off his highest-graded game of the season against the Dallas Cowboys last week.
In Tennessee's 51-30 loss to Dallas on Sunday , Schlottmann surrendered one quarterback pressure, tallied an 80.3 PFF grade , including an 82.2 run-blocking mark, and didn't commit a penalty for the second straight contest. The 31-year-old is making the Titans' decision to sign him to a cheap, low-risk contract a savvy move.
Even after signing Schlottmann in March, the Titans selected Pat Coogan in the sixth round of April's draft, likely with plans to eventually hand the Indiana product the starting gig . However, if Schlottmann continues to be one of the more impactful contributors on Brian Daboll's offense, Tennessee will have to seriously consider naming him the 2027 starting center and keeping Coogan on the bench.
The Titans will look to capture their second win of the season this weekend at EverBank Stadium against the Jacksonville Jaguars. We'll see if Schlottmann can turn in another steady outing and help Tennessee get back in the win column after dropping two in a row coming out of the bye.
Dharya Sharma is a sportswriter from Nebraska who has been covering the Tennessee Titans through his website, SharmSports, since 2023. He is also an NFL and NBA writer for The Sporting News and had a previous stop with Sportsnaut. Follow him on X @SharmSports

title: Why Any Smoke Around Robert Saleh's Job is Way Too Premature for Titans
full_text:
Today, in reporting NFL head coaches potentially on the hot seat, ESPN's Jeremy Fowler mentioned Robert Saleh toward the end of his update. The Tennessee Titans head coach hasn't been mentioned in any sort of "could-be-fired" capacity, so his sudden drop here came as a surprise.
"Tennessee seems like one to watch because of the Titans' penchant for firings in recent years. I'm curious whether Tennessee breaks precedent and gives Robert Saleh time..." Fowler wrote. "The a 51-30 loss to Dallas prompted Saleh to call his defense "dogs---" in a news conference. I'm not sure where to go with that, but what I'm saying is Tennessee is usually a wild card based on recent history."
This appears to be nothing more than smoke on the surface, but Fowler's reptuation demands Titans fans at least give this one a look. It wasn't all that long ago that Brian Callahan was fired for producing just four wins in 23 games.
Saleh has one in 10. Could a one-season firing actually be in the cards?
Probably not. There are a number of reasons why Saleh's scenario is different than Callahan's; perhaps the most notable of which is that he didn't get his say at a QB. Cam Ward was drafted under a waning Callahan regime. So were WRs Elic Ayomanor and Chimere Dike, among others.
Not only that, but Callahan took a franchise that wasn't far removed from success under Mike Vrabel and lowered the bar to levels the team hadn't seen in years. Saleh inherited a far worse scenario than Callahan, and the early returns (despite the win column) are more promising.
Ward and the offense are developing at a rapid pace. Tennessee traded two key defenders for draft capital that could turn this team around in the matter of an offseason. Saleh also recently said he has "100% support" from Titans owner Amy Adams Strunk.
Take that for what it's worth, but two-year-or-less firing and hiring cycles don't get a team anywhere. The process has to be waited out at some point, and this feels like the perfect juncture for Tennessee.
A 1-16 finish would likely mean otherwise, but with the Colts, a post-Aaron Rodgers Steelers team, the Commanders, and the Raiders coming up, Tennessee is almost bound to get lucky a time or two.
Let's say Saleh finishes this season 3-14, just as Callahan did in his first year. Do you fire him when you didn't fire Callahan? Or do you let him see it through one more season, equipped with two first-round picks and a QB who is trending to have settled into his role by then.
The Titans' rebuild depends on those last two points, no matter who is steering the ship. With Ward getting better and GM Mike Borgonzi gearing up for his most important draft in the position, the whole process is simply bigger than Saleh.
Whether or not he's the solution is hard to tell, especially with this roster, but it's far too early to know if he's the problem. As of now, Titans fans should treat this season as a trial run for what Saleh could bring to the table in 2027.
Maybe we revisit this discussion then. Right now, however, there's no fire to the smoke.

title: Titans' Search for Help in Secondary Gets Desperate With New Signing — But it Still Isn't Enough
full_text:
Today, the Tennessee Titans signed CB Corey Thornton off the Carolina Panthers' practice squad. This comes one day after Tennessee signed offseason-regular DB Derrick Canteen to their own practice squad, signaling a mad rush to plug their game-losing gaps in the secondary.
Robert Saleh's defense has allowed 40+ points in three straight games. In all three, opposing QBs threw for more than 300 yards and downright picked on the Titans' CBs. With Cor'Dale Flott leaving this past week with a neck injury, a bad thing got even worse. This unit looks unplayable.
I'm not here to knock the front office for trying to find temporary solutions therein. Truth be told, I actually like Thornton as a pickup at this stage in the season. He logged an eye-popping interception with the Panthers earlier this month, and is just 25 years old and in his second NFL season.
He fits the bill in Tennessee, particularly regarding what this team is trying to become over the next few years. The younger the Titans get, the better. But a likable signing is not enough for a 1-9 football team that has no greater struggle than the one in the secondary. It's too little, far too late.
This past offseason, Tennessee went all out to sign Flott, as well as CBs Alontae Taylor and Joshua Williams. It was played off as an expensive effort to fast-track Saleh's defense to success. In retrospect, it's hard to stomach just how much money was apparently wasted.
Between the three defenders, Tennessee chunked out $111 million. Per PFF, both Taylor (107th) and Williams (101st) are in the bottom tier of 108 players at their position. Flott's overall grade is hardly better, ranking 80th. At least he has two picks this season.
Whether it comes in the draft or by way of cheaper, much more fortunate signings in the future, the Titans are going to have to chip away at the disastrous structure they've built downfield. This is an issue bound to persist for the rest of this season, at least.
I don't need to be the one to tell you that fringe additions heading into Week 12 won't completely fix this team's problems. However, even when Flott returns and if Taylor plays the rest of this season at nickel (his strong suit), you're looking at an incomplete puzzle.
The Titans got it wrong this past offseason as far as the secondary goes. I hope Thornton comes onto the scene and carves out a significant role. Even then, though, it would make the millions Tennessee spent on their current group look even worse.
Band-aids over broken bridges. This one is going to take time in Nashville.

title: Why the Titans Will Beat the Jaguars in Week 12, Why They Won't, and a Prediction
full_text:
The Tennessee Titans winning on the road in Jacksonville in Week 12 would mark their least-likely win of the season. DraftKings Sportsbook has the line set at 14.5 in favor of the Jaguars; that's a whole two touchdowns. After the Titans' 51-30 loss last week, maybe they're not all that far off.
Tennessee's offense could do their part once again, only for Robert Saleh's defense to allow 40+ points and result in yet another loss for the Titans. Jacksonville at least looked beatable in Nashville two weeks ago, however, and that's enough to make this interesting.
That leads us to this week's will, won't, prediction. Here's one reason the Titans will beat the Jaguars, one reason they won't, and my own prediction.
The Titans offense has scored 23 or more points in five straight games, and more than 30 in two of their last three. Cam Ward's unit is operating at a season-best, and if Tennessee wins in Week 12, it'll be because they finally overcome their own defensive shortcomings.
This is a Titans vs. Titans scenario, but that's how it has been for Tennessee in recent weeks. It's a matter of getting out of their own way and, for once, trying to piece together a semi-complete game.
Jacksonville will have All-Pro S Jessie Bates this time around, after he missed the Titans' first meeting due to having just been traded to the Jaguars. It appears more likely now Ward has a good game than not, which is enough progress for the offense to be pinned as the Titans' winning factor.
This is a weirder reason, but something about the Jaguars' latest loss to the New York Giants and J.J. McCarthy tells me they won't be sprinting to repeat it. Great teams rarely lose back-to-back, especially not when the modern Titans are involved.
I just don't see a 7-3, Super-Bowl-contending Jacksonville team returning to their home field off that loss without some anger. The Jaguars' 18 points last Sunday was also the first time they'd scored less than 30 since October 11.
It's bad timing for a Tennessee team coming off their own defeat, but the motivation is different on either side. A loss for Jacksonville mars an ongoing playoff chase, while a loss for the Titans pushes them closer to the first overall pick.
From the outside looking in, it's the perfect storm for a nasty divisional game for the road team.
That leads us here. I try to balance the two perspectives in this series with my prediction, and the silver lining here is that the Titans' defense finally holds a team to less than 40 points. Elsewhere, though, don't expect any surprises.
Cam Ward puts on another promising, low-mistake performance. Tennessee's defense gets ripped by Lawrence and the Jags just enough to keep the Titans out of it most of the way through. Not necessarily a blowout (coming in right under the spread), but not a close contest, either.
These two teams were worlds apart in Week 10, and one game in two weeks isn't enough to change that. I've got the Jaguars coming out on top, but if Ward keeps climbing, Titans fans should happily pocket his improvement and press on regardless.

title: Titans' Snap Count Analysis in Week 11: Reserve WRs Show Out, While Secondary Takes Another Hit
full_text:
After losing 51-30 in blowout fashion to the Dallas Cowboys on the road, the lowly Tennessee Titans fall to 1-9 for the second consecutive season.
Currently, the Titans are in possession of the No. 1 pick in the NFL Draft, edging out fellow one-win teams the Los Angeles Chargers and the Miami Dolphins due to strength of schedule. Tennessee may consider losing more in order to lock in the coveted top pick.
It's time for the weekly breakdown of the decisions made by the Robert Saleh-led coaching staff, both the good and the bad, based on players' snaps. Unsurprisingly, the offense remains in the driver's seat. We'll touch on the fun stuff first.
Against the Cowboys, WR Chimere Dike was QB Cam Ward's favorite target, leading the Titans in receptions and receiving yards. Dike caught six of seven targets for 69 yards. This marks Dike's second game in three weeks with at least 60-plus receiving yards and five-plus receptions.
In the previous week, Dike recorded 54 snaps against Jacksonville, and he played 53 in Dallas. Not to mention his role as a returner on special teams, Dike had six returns for 127 yards, which totals more than 200 all-purpose yards on the day.
Already, in his second season, Dike has climbed to sixth all-time for the most kick return yards in franchise history with 2,700 yards.
Earlier in the season, the 23-year-old receiver had a limited role, only recording six receptions in the first seven weeks of the season. However, Dike has been entrusted with a larger role in the offense, especially with rookie standout WR Carnell Tate being sidelined for two games nursing an injury, and he's proven himself recently.
It's been an odd year for WR Calvin Ridley. Prior to playing the Cowboys, he only had six catches for 91 yards. The Titans were open about trying to deal the aging receiver ahead of the NFL trade deadline, but there were no takers. Against Jacksonville, Ridley only played four snaps, and it looked like the Titans were moving on from him in favor of the practice squad call-up Xavier Restrepo.
In Dallas, Ridley had took an unexpected leap and made an impact despite only playing 26 snaps. He caught five passes for 68 yards, including a touchdown on a miraculous play from Ward , who escaped Cowboys defenders to find Ridley in the back corner of the end zone on a fourth and long.
It was Ridley's first game of 60-plus receiving yards and a touchdown since Week 16 of 2024 , nearly two years ago.
Nearing age 32, Ridley's best days are more than likely behind him. To be fair, most of his touches in this contest came in garbage time. But he still played his best game of the season by recording season highs in receptions and receiving yards, as well as scoring his first touchdown of the year. Improvement is improvement for a player that had been obsolete.
After trading away two defensive pillars in DT Jeffery Simmons and S Amani Hooker ahead of the NFL trade deadline, the Titans' defense has taken a significant step backward. For the third week in a row, Tennessee has allowed 40-plus points.
Furthermore, the Titans' secondary has allowed at least one opposing receiver 100 or more yards in four straight games.
Against Dallas, CB Joshua Williams led the Titans with a team-high 11 tackles but allowed a game-high 92 receiving yards and eight catches on 10 targets, according to PFF . Williams was one of four Titans to play all 65 defensive snaps.
In the week prior against Jacksonville, Williams played all 74 defensive snaps and allowed 86 yards and six receptions. Playing a ton of snaps doesn't make a player a snap winner.
The Cowboys' duo of WR Ceedee Lamb and WR George Pickens combined for 18 catches, 234 receiving yards, and two touchdowns. Opposing receivers are continuing to find success against Williams, who hasn't recorded a pass breakup since his season debut in Week 6, which is extremely concerning for someone who, again, plays every snap.
Tennessee making a change seems like the obvious fix. But after Amani Hooker was traded at the deadline and Cor'Dale Flott left in Week 11 with a neck injury, this may just be a matter of waiting until the 2027 NFL Draft... at the earliest.

title: How Titans Wasted No Time Crowning a New WR2 After Wan'Dale Robinson's Move to IR
full_text:
No position group on the Tennessee Titans is as packed with young talent as the WR room. Cam Ward's climb in the latter half of this season is owed in large part to his varied cast of weapons that only seem to get better as the age decreases on the depth chart.
Carnell Tate is inarguably the team's WR1 at this point, taking the role almost as soon as he came onto the scene as a rookie this year. That left $70 million offseason pickup Wan'Dale Robinson in the team's WR2 slot, but his struggles and eventual move to IR opened that door wide.
The result in Week 11 was a decisive takeover from Florida product Chimere Dike. We made the case prior to kickoff that Dike should be heavily involved in the slot in place of Robinson, and that came to pass in an exciting way despite a loss to the Dallas Cowboys.
Dike's 54 snaps were second on the team only to Tate's 62. Elic Ayomanor trailed on the outside with 37, followed by Calvin Ridley (26) and Xavier Restrepo (17). Dike hit a season-high 60% slot rate without Robinson in rotation.
The clear separation lies with the Titans' fourth overall pick, and their only playmaker in the WR core to achieve Pro Bowl honors.
Those were for his impact on special teams, sure, but Dike stepping into a larger role as a pass-catcher in this offense is best-case scenario. The same speed and vision that make him an elite returner also mean he's a swift, effective route runner.
Dike is a Swiss Army knife, and the Titans should be using that to their full advantage now and in the future. His six receptions for 69 yards led the team vs. the Cowboys. Compared to Robinson, Dike has 209 yards to Robinson's 272, and that's on half of the latter's 38 receptions.
It's also necessary to point out that Dike has generated those numbers on far fewer snaps in the passing game, too; he wasn't even a play-to-play option in that way when the season began. This is a recent emergence, though it's great that Tennessee didn't waste time implementing Dike.
No matter what move the Titans make with their top pick in next year's draft or how Robinson performs when he returns, Dike is a proven fixture of this offense's success. He should be kept around, and further, pushed into the spotlight.
The dude has what it takes. All he needs are consistent chances to prove it, and zips from Cam Ward downfield.

title: Ranking 4 Top Prospects Titans Could Take With First Overall Pick in 2027 Draft
full_text:
If you're reading this, we don't have to tell you how important the 2027 NFL Draft is for the Tennessee Titans. Not only is it a crucial interval for HC Robert Saleh and GM Mike Borgonzi to prove their collective vision, but it's a window of opportunity for this rebuild to actually take the next step.
As of now, the 1-9 Titans hold the first overall pick next spring. That would be the second time in three years, and QB Cam Ward rapidly improving is starting to make that selection look like a great investment. Tennessee needs an even better, more immediately beneficial pick this time around.
Based on ESPN's big board - which is almost a consensus for teams not in the QB market - I'm ranking the four most realistic targets the Titans could spend their top pick on if they end up securing it by the end of the season.
If I were in Borgonzi's shoes, here's how I'd assess the ladder of candidates at the top of the list.
Jeremiah Smith is the biggest no-brainer to pass through the draft in years, and it'd be shocking if the Titans (or any team, for that matter) passed up on him.
Smith's 17 touchdowns and 1,482 yards are both good for the best in college football this season. The big-body receiver, and former teammate of Carnell Tate, is as elite a route runner as they come. He excels at outrunning defenders and going up for contested catches over them.
In short, Smith can do it all. The only drawback of this selection is the pitiful state of Saleh's defense after DT Jeffery Simmons and S Amani Hooker were traded, but with another first-rounder and two picks in the second, Tennessee could make up defensive ground after taking Smith if they wished.
Colin Simmons is my favorite defensive prospect in this draft, and is perhaps the most obvious "don't overthink it" prospect on the board. The Texas EDGE is a good ol' fashioned star.
In his junior year with the Longhorns, Simmons has amassed 10.5 sacks (good for fifth nationally), as well as 2 forced fumbles and 32 total tackles. He's a wrecking ball off the edge, exhibiting lighting speed and versatility at 6'3", 246 lbs.
Simmons has a great burst, shifty footwork, and all the makings of a long-term defensive cornerstone. This is his second straight season with 10+ sacks, and he had nine as a freshman. If the Titans don't go Smith, Simmons is my top option for a pivot.
If the Titans are after an EDGE and Colin Simmons isn't the choice, South Carolina's Dylan Stewart is essentially a lateral move to the same dominant end.
Stewart is taller and more trim than Simmons, at 6'5", 250 lbs, and not quite as outright explosive on the sack front - he has 2.5 on the season. But with three forced fumbles and 18 pressures, the Gamecock is a sleeping giant and one-on-one nightmare.
He overpowers linemen with ease and slips tackles with impressive, quick footwork. Stewart is agile, long, and another player that would be difficult for any GM in need of an explosive defender to overthink. I may prefer Simmons on the page, but the Titans would have a winner in either.
Finally, we'll pivot slightly to the CB position with Leonard Moore, out of Notre Dame. Moore has been widely considered the top CB in the 2027 class, and it's arguable that the Titans need more help in the secondary than anywhere else.
However, between the money Tennessee spent at CB this past offseason and the undeniable prowess of the three prospects above him, I'd rather see the Titans take a swing at this position later in the draft or in free agency than with their top selection.
In last year's College Football Playoff, Moore held the aforementioned Smith to one catch on two targets, and just seven receiving yards. This season, Moore has forced one fumble and defended seven passes. He's failed to produce an INT through 11 games after nabbing five last year.
Teams don't throw to Moore for a reason. He's a rock-solid prospect with the physical tools to go far in the NFL, and even if the Titans went a surprising route and chose him out of this batch, it would be far from the end of the world.
The 2027 pool of players is just that good, and the Titans are poised to have their pick of the lot. They'd almost have to try to mess this one up at first overall.
Lane covers the Tennessee Titans, where he brings an evolving team's journey to fans on a daily basis. A longtime sports fanatic and recent baby blue jersey aficionado.

title: 5 Things Commanders Fans Can Be Thankful For This Thanksgiving—and 1 Problem They Can’t Ignore
full_text:
As we all sit down for Thanksgiving dinner today, everyone has things to be thankful for, and exactly what varies from person to person. For fans of the Burgundy and Gold, it all starts with the direction the franchise is currently heading. Washington fans aren't dumb and can see right through empty promises made by those in executive positions. They've been scarred by years of "getting it right" under several different coaching staffs, so when one goes 1-4-1 to start year three, they tend to stop listening. Since that start, though, the Commanders have gone 3-1 and are coming off a 22-20 walk-off win over what was the hottest team in the NFL, the Cincinnati Bengals. Then, Wednesday brought an agreement to sign former All-Pro receiver Brandon Aiyuk to the practice squad.
Big things are centered around D.C. and Washington Football again. The 2027 NFL Draft is coming to the nation's capital on April 29–May 1. League and team officials unveiled a countdown clock at Union Station on Monday , with the draft itself planned around the National Mall. The District has also advanced a plan for the RFK campus that includes a proposed new Commanders stadium, with early development expected within the year, as the stadium is scheduled to open in 2030.
Washington is 4-5-1, but take a look at who’s next. The Commanders visit Arizona (3-8) and Tennessee (1-9) before coming home to face Houston (4-6) and Atlanta (3-7). Arizona fired defensive coordinator Nick Rallis on Monday , and quarterback Carson Beck missed Wednesday’s practice with back spasms. Josh Johnson is preparing to start if Beck can’t play. None of that wins Sunday’s game for Washington, but if the Commanders can’t improve their record over the next month, it’ll be hard to blame the schedule.
For all the things fans have had reason to complain about this season, giving the ball away hasn’t been high on the list. Washington has turned it over seven times in 10 games and taken it away 14, leaving the Commanders at plus-seven, tied for second in the NFL. Neither team had a turnover Monday, so that margin stayed right where it was. Being 4-5-1 with those numbers tells you there are still things to fix, but at least Washington isn’t handing opponents extra possessions.
Sonny Styles has played every game and leads Washington with 85 tackles. He’s also made five tackles for loss and has a sack, an interception, and a forced fumble. Those aren’t numbers the Commanders are waiting for him to reach someday; he’s put them up in the first 10 games of his career. Antonio Williams caught nine passes for 122 yards Monday, bringing him to 37 receptions for 448 yards and two touchdowns. Drew Stevens made all five of his field-goal attempts against Cincinnati and has hit 19 of his last 20; the NFL named him NFC Special Teams Player of the Week. Williams and Stevens are also two of the four nominees for Pepsi NFL Rookie of the Week. Washington has a rookie leading the team in tackles, another leading it in receiving yards, and a kicker who just won a game as time expired. That’s a lot to get from one class this early.
individual player runouts 📈 pic.twitter.com/dLxQkeM7Od
Say what you will, but as my grandfather always told my sister and me, the proof is in the pudding. And when the game is on the line, Daniels flips the switch and hits another level. It's like he gets better when the pressure goes up. Against the Bengals on Monday, Daniels threw for 289 yards and rushed for 55 without turning the ball over. With only 39 seconds and no timeouts to work with, his two completions to Antonio Williams gained all 64 yards Washington needed to set up Drew Stevens’ winning kick. Commanders head coach Dan Quinn framed it perfectly: "It's not on second-and-1 in the second quarter, but it is in the fourth quarter when the game's on the line. And that is when I feel him come to fully express who he is." Commanders fans may not have everything, but when the game comes down to one possession, they can relax knowing they have JD5. One honest concern since Terry McLaurin's season-ending injury is the receiver room and how much actual talent the team has. Washington made a move Wednesday that looks to improve that situation with a player Daniels already knows: Brandon Aiyuk, with the two already spending time together in college at Arizona State. Aiyuk hasn't played an NFL snap since October 2024, though, and Washington still has to find out how much of his old form is left.
Washington moved the ball well enough Monday to do something no NFL team had done in 45 seasons: finish with six straight scoring drives of at least 50 yards . How did that produce just one touchdown? The Commanders went 1-for-4 in the red zone. A false start at Cincinnati’s 13 turned second-and-9 into second-and-14 on one trip, and another reached first-and-goal at the 8 before ending in a field goal. Drew Stevens’ final kick was exactly what Washington needed. Those earlier trips are why they needed him to win the game with no time left. title: Commanders-Cardinals Injury Report: Amik Robertson’s Ankle Revives Washington’s Cornerback Question
full_text:
The Washington Commanders released their first injury report of Week 12 , and while it lists several players, only three carry serious weight right now. Cornerback Amik Robertson was listed as an estimated nonparticipant Wednesday with an injured ankle; receiver Treylon Burks (foot) and defensive lineman Charles Omenihu (rib) were limited, while Stefon Diggs was listed as a nonparticipant for personal reasons. Robertson hurt his ankle on the last play of Friday’s practice and was inactive Monday against Cincinnati . With him out, Rasul Douglas and Trey Amos played all 58 defensive snaps. Fabian Moreau played 10, and Mike Sainristil got four. Thursday’s report will tell us whether Robertson is any closer to playing Sunday. Jayden Daniels’ left hand appeared on the report alongside his left elbow, but he was listed as full. Head coach Dan Quinn said Daniels banged up his non-throwing hand on a scramble against Cincinnati and had some swelling. Quinn said Tuesday that “ it wasn't anything that limited him .” Burks played 49 offensive snaps Monday, and Omenihu played 31 on defense before appearing on this report with a rib issue. Rachaad White (heel) and Sonny Styles (ankle) were listed as full, as were John Bates (shoulder), Quan Martin (shoulder), Andrew Wylie (hip), and Colson Yankoff (knee). White had been questionable against Cincinnati but played. Washington has not issued any game designations for Sunday.
Arizona has its own quarterback question. Carson Beck (back) didn’t practice Wednesday, and head coach Mike LaFleur said Josh Johnson is preparing for another start if Beck can’t play. Beck remains day-to-day. Guard Jon Gaines II (ankle) also sat out after a setback, while linebacker Cody Simon (calf) was limited. Both teams will update their reports Thursday before listing game designations Friday.
